items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I apologise to the House that I have
not had a chance to talk to my colleagues a bout this, but I seek leave to move without
debate and without notice acknowledgment of, and condolences for, the death of a New
Zealand soldier, John Howard, in Afghanistan  while serving with the British Parachute
Regiment.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? There is none.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I move, That this House note with sadness the loss of New
Zealander Private John Howard, serving wi th the British Parachute Regiment in
Afghanistan, and offer its condolences to his parents, Roger Howard and Anne Scott,
family, and friends.
Motion agreed to.
Tax System Changes—Effect on New Zealanders
1. Hon PHIL GOFF (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that the “vast majority” of New Zealanders will be “better off” as
a result of the tax switch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because the combination of putting up
GST, increasing superannuation, benefits, and Working for Families payments, and
cutting income tax rates across the board have  made people demonstrably better off. Of
course, I guess the proof of this policy working is that there is not one political party
that is campaigning on reversing the tax switch.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: How are the vast majority of Ne w Zealanders better off when the
household economic survey released recently by the Government Statistician shows that
the average household income in the year  to June 2010 for New Zealand households
dropped by $28 a week, and that individuals were each $17 a week worse off?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As we have been through this question several times before, I
will give the Leader of the Opposition the same answer as previously, which is that it is
a very broad measure of inco me and it is not solely normal income. It includes
investment income and a lot of other issues.
15906 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: How many New Zealanders got wages increases in the last year that
matched the 5.1 percent increase in food prices in the year to October 2010 and the 20
percent increase in vegetable prices in the September quarter alone?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot answer in relation to what individuals got in pay
increases; I simply do not see the pay packets of 2.5 million full-time New Zealand
workers. But what I do know is that real after-tax incomes have grown by about 8
percent in the time that National has been in  Government and grew by 3 percent in the
entire 9 years that Labour was last in offi ce. I also add that f ood prices, up until the
point that I am looking at, at  the moment, were actually do wn by 2 percent at 3 June,
compared with much higher food prices under the previous Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I seek leave to table a Government document showing that food
prices in the last year went up, in fact, by 5.1 percent, and that vegetable prices went up
by 20 percent.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Could the member be more specific about what the document is?

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: The documents are both publications by New Zealand Government
agencies—the Government Statistician, I think. I will have a look at the papers; I have
them with me. Statistics New Zealand is the source of the figures. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is my fault, and I accept the blame for this exchange happening. It
should not happen. We do not norma lly table current or recent releases from Statistics
New Zealand, because every member has them.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: Where did the idea for the tax switch come from?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am proud to say we thought of  it all by ourselves, with a
little help from some advisers. We did not have to google Ed Miliband’s statements and
shamelessly plagiarise them, like Phil Go ff did with his “squeezed middle” speech.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to the member. Can we have a little order, please, so
that at least the Speaker can hear the question?

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Are the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research, economist
Bill Rosenberg, and Treasury’s own figures all wrong in showing that for middle and
lower-income New Zealanders prices have in creased, and continue to increase, faster
than wages?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Stand up, “David Cameron”.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: For a start, no. I get my Davids  right, I tell Trevor Mallard. I
come back to the business at hand. No, the incr ease in real after-tax wages is 8 percent.
But let us look at those middle-income New Zealanders, because it is  quite interesting.
When we look at middle-income New Zealande rs and at the tax that they pay, we can
see that under the National Government their personal ta x rate has halved from 33
percent to 17.5 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Are more than half of the New Zealanders in recent surveys wrong
in stating that they are worse off after the tax switch, and is the Pr ime Minister telling
them that, contrary to what they think, they are actually better off?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not one to go out and criticise polls. But if the member is
quoting from the HorizonPoll, which he is, an d if he seriously believes that Winston
Peters is on 6 percent and he is on 28 percent, then he is underestimating even his
performance in other public polls.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: He’s very worried, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The House is having a bit of fun, but I ask m
embers to treat
question time with a little more respect than that.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: How does he expect anyone to belie ve that real incomes are rising,
when today’s figures show that manufacturing sales in this country are at a 10-year low
and that housing consents are 20 percent down from what they were earlier this year,
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15907
and retailers are comprehensively saying they are facing the worst situation in decades,
simply because wage earners and salary earners do not have money in their pockets to
spend?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am glad the member raised that, because there is an article
on the front page of this morning’s “Busin ess Herald” about Paymark and what it is
seeing in terms of consumer spending. The article indicated that spending had increased
by 5.5 percent. When Paymark was asked in  November why that was happening, the
answer from the chief executive was: “Oh, because New Zealanders have more money
as a result of the tax cuts, and they’re out there spending it.”

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I seek the leave of the House to  table a document that the Prime
Minister has not seen, which shows that ma nufacturing sales volumes continue to fall—
the lowest level for more than 10 years. It is from Statistics New Zealand.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There is a proper process for seek ing leave to table documents, and
it does not include comments about whether the Prime Minister may have seen them.
The member should identify the source of the do cument before saying what is in it. The
habit of saying what is in a document, when there is no real document to be tabled, is
not good enough.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That is out of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Members will be l eaving the House. [Interruption ] The member
will be very careful. The member will leave the Chamber. I will not tolerate that.
Hon Trevor Mallard withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The House will come to order. What I was saying was being said
for good reason. There are times when members s eek leave to table a document that is
clearly outside the current rules for tabli ng documents, but they want to get across a
political point. That is why I require members to identify the source of the document, so
that members can make a proper decision on it. I will allow the member to seek leave
again to table his document.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. I take offence at the implication
that I was seeking to table a document that does not exist. I have it in my hand. It was
out of order for you to make that allegation.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will seek leave, if he wishes to, to table his document.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think that your comments were
out of order in implying that I wanted to table—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am on my feet. The Leader of the Opposition will resume his seat.
If he wishes to stay in the House, he will show the Speaker respect. I have invited him
to seek leave again properly to table his document. He does not need to take that
opportunity, but he is welcome to do so if he wishes.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. I do respect your role as
Speaker, and I expect you to respect the members of this House and their integrity when
you make comments like that, which reflect on it. I do not think that is good enough.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member should just reflect on the way that he sought leave to
table the document. The member, when seek ing leave to table the document, made a
comment about whether the Prime Minister had seen it. He then went on to say what the
document contained—in other words, the point s that he wanted to make—instead of
first identifying where the document was from. That is not good enough, and that is why
I clamped down on what the member was doing. If the member took offence at that, I
apologise to him for the offence caused. But I am serious about the way that members
will seek leave to table documents, and I am  serious about the respect that will be
shown in this House. Any further nonsense today will be treated just as firmly as I have
treated the Hon Trevor Mallard—and that includes party leaders.
15908 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I seek leave to table a document  from Statistics New Zealand, the
Acting Government Statistician, dated toda y, which shows that manufacturing sales
volumes are at the lowest level for more than 10 years.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: All members have the release from  Statistics New Zealand. We do
not seek leave to table those kinds of documents.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. You have made that comment
on two occasions today. I cannot remember your previously ruling out documents by
Government agencies. You have ruled out press statements. Are you setting a new
precedent today?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will know that the pr ocess for seeking leave to table
documents, and for the House to consider th e tabling of documents, is intended to
provide members with information that th ey do not have. All members have been
circulated that information today. All members have that information, so there is
absolutely no point in wasting the time of the House. It is clearly an attempt to make a
political point, and that is not what the tabling of documents is about. We have
established that very clearly. It is about providing information for the House: providing
members with information that they otherw ise would not have access to. That is why I
am not seeking leave for that matter.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek your clarification
on this matter. If I interpre t it correctly, your previous ruling was made because the
release in question was available on the Internet to members, whether they had sought it
or not. I seek your clarification of wh ether you are now ruling that any document
released generally on the Internet, or available on the Internet, is una ble to be tabled in
the House, because that would be a significant extension of your previous ruling in
respect of media statements.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I just ask members to look back at  the relevant Standing Order. The
provision is there to provide members with access to information that they otherwise
would not have. Clearly, in the case of recen t releases from Statis tics New Zealand, all
members have them, and that is why I am not seeking leave for that purpose.
Financial Performance, Government—Improvements
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What steps is the Government taking to improve its financial performance?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is taking steps to
improve its management of cap ital expenditure. Total assets  of the Crown have trebled
over the past decade to more than $223 billion at June 2010, yet the means by which
those are funded and the way that the capit al is used is not transparent to the
Government, let alone to the taxpayer. Yest erday the Government released the first
annual portfolio report, which is a concise summary of the financial performance of
Crown financial institutions, State-owned enterprises, and Crown research institutes.
Next week we will release the Crown’s first investment statement, which will show in
full the Government’s balance sheet and its investment intentions over the next 5 years.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What does the 2010 annual portfolio report show?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The portfolio report sets out the performance of, in
particular, State-owned enterprises. Excluding the rail and post enterprises, State-owned
enterprises earned $500 million and declared dividends of $386 million. Crown
financial institutions collectively returned 12.8 percent last year, following 2 years of
losses. By the end of the year the Crown had $40 billion invested in financial
investments, and the Crown has around $700 m illion invested in the Crown research
institutes.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: W
hat will the 2010 investment statement show?
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15909

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The investment statement will show the quantity of
Government assets and the ambition of th e Government’s investment programme to
2015. Net Crown assets are expected to grow by some $35 billion over the next 4 years,
and total investment is around $70 billion of  fresh capital investment over the next 4
years. About half of that relates to services  such as schools, hosp itals, rail, broadband,
roads, and the electricity network. There is also a substantial accumulation within the
Crown’s investments funds, which are expe cted to grow by about $20 billion of
investments through to 2015.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: How can he claim to be improving the Government’s net
financial position when his deficit has increas ed in the last quarter alone by almost $2
billion more than forecast?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the first place, the figures I have been talking about are
the asset values of the Government, whereas the deficit relates to our operating
expenditure. But the member does make a fair point that the Government cannot
continue to run very large deficits. This year it coul d be somewhere up to $11 billion.
We have set out a path to reach a surplus by 2015. That will take some very significant
fiscal discipline, which I know the member is  opposed to, but it is the only way we will
get there.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Further to the Minister’s answ er to question No. 8 yesterday,
when he said he would not be  surprised if there were some  quarters in the last 2 years
when annualised real GDP per capita had fa llen, can he now confirm that, in fact,
annualised real GDP per capita has fallen in every single quarter si nce his Government
took office, meaning that average New Zealan ders have consistently gone backwards,
and are still earning less today, on average, than on the day he first took office?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I disagree with the member’s last point. But as I pointed
out yesterday, in a significant recession one would expect real per capita incomes to
drop. The Government has set out a plan to turn that round. However, we are dealing
with the legacy of a Government that mana ged to have negative growth in real per
capita incomes even when the rest of the wo rld was not in recession and the rest of the
world was growing strongly. I do not know how he managed it.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I seek leave to table the statis tical table from page 8 of the
monthly economic indicators published by Tr easury, which shows that real GDP per
capita has fallen every single quarter since the Government took office up until—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Why does the Government need to lift the quality of its investment
performance?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Because we are dealing with the legacy of 10 years when the
previous Government spent large amounts on  new capital. Much of that was spent
ineffectively. The attention paid to it by the Public Service has been  just about zero, so
we are going through a signifi cant exercise to make sure taxpayers get value for the
$230 billion of assets that they own.
Point of Order—Withdrawal of Member

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek some
guidance as to when Mr Mallard can return. I w ould seek that he be able to return at the
end of question time.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, he is out for the day.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: That’s pretty tough.
15910 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No one will comment on a Speaker’s ruling. Members know that I
do not throw many members out of this Chamber, but they are out for the day when I do
ask them to leave.
Tax Cuts—Fairness and Impact on Economic Growth
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he
stand by his statement that “Our tax cuts have been good for economic growth and fair
for New Zealanders.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, the tax cuts were part of a
fiscally neutral package, which was designed to tilt the incentives in this economy away
from excessive housing speculation and ex cessive consumption, which were both
funded by excessive debt, and to create more incentives for savings, investment,
exports, and new jobs. We are satisfied that the package we put together, when we take
into account the increases in GST and the decreases in income taxes, is fair for New
Zealanders, and in the long run will be good for economic growth.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister consider extending Working for Families tax
credits to families who are reliant on benefits, as a way of both stimulating the economy
and promoting fairness; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member will know, the previous Government
extended Working for Families considerably and introduced a mechanism that ensured
that people with children who went from bene fits into work were better off for being in
work. By and large, the Government has left that mechanism in place and has not seen a
strong case for making significant changes to it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Minister aware of the ev idence from the US Congressional
Budget Office that putting more money in th e back pockets of beneficiaries has the
biggest stimulus effect on the economy b ecause low-income households spend all the
money they get on essentials?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I am aware of that evidence. The Government has
worked to strike a balance between the need to protect New Zealanders as much as
possible from the sharp edges of recession—and  in the case of beneficiaries we have
made sure there have been adjustments to be nefits regardless of the economic situation,
including compensation for GST increases—a nd on the other hand the need to make
sure we do not end up in the situation of a country like Ireland, where we lose control of
our economic destiny because we have not liv ed within our means. So the Government
has stimulated the economy in the recession, but now has a path back to surplus.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister agree that extending Working for Families tax
credits, as proposed in the Green Party’s Mind the Gap plan, w ould inject $300 million
into the economy, and give 130,000 low-income families a much-needed income boost?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I would not dispute the facts with the member; I am sure she
has done her research. As I have said, though, we  have tried to strike a balance between
supporting people through the recession, and on the other hand showing a path back to
surplus. There is any amount of spending we  could do right now, but we would simply
have to pay it back later, and on any signi ficant scale it would pose a risk to New
Zealand’s economic future.

items.speaker: Nikki Kaye
items.text: Has he seen any reports on economic support for middle-income New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I have seen some reports. One was a speech entitled
“The Squeezed Middle”. Another was a statement that says: “My aim is to show our
party is on the side of the squeezed middle …” . The first one was the title of a speech
by Phil Goff; the second one was a statem ent made about 9 weeks before by Ed
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15911
Miliband in the UK, and I do not think it was an accident that they used the same
language.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he stand by his statement made in public session to the
Finance and Expenditure Committee on 27 October 2010 when he said, in relation to a
question about fiscally irresponsible tax cu ts: “Despite the recession, we implemented
the first tranche of that because we said we would”, and can he confirm that he admitted
to the Finance and Expenditure Committee that “this has had a $1.5 billion impact on
tax revenue”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is a matter of fact that National promised a series of tax
cuts in the 2008 election. We implemented the first tranche of those and we cancelled
the next two, because between announcing the package and the implementation date
Lehman Brothers crashed and the world went  into a global financial crisis. So we
chopped off the last two tranches of that tax cut.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Respectfully, I do not
believe that the Minister has addressed th e essence of that question. The question was
not whether he passed $1.5 billion in tax cuts, but whether he did so knowing that that
would be irresponsible because of the recession. I do not believe he has answered that
point.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not think, though, th at the member can expect the Minister to
give exactly the answer the member might want. The member asked him about the issue
of those tax cuts, specifically, and the Mini ster replied with w hy the Government had
implemented the first tranche, and why it had not implemented the rest. The member
has further supplementary questions if he wishes to pursue the matter.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister not agree that every child should have the
essentials this Christmas, regardless of whether their parent relies on the benefit?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, that would be desirable.  One of the reasons we set up
the Welfare Working Group is that there is a strong correlation between child poverty
and people who are long term on benefits. That  is why I hope the Gr een Party will give
full consideration to the recommendations of that working-group when they come
forward early in the new year. We all have an interest in ensuring that the large
proportion of New Zealand children who are raised in child poverty can have more hope
than a lifetime of dependency.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table two documents . The first is a paper from the US
Congressional Budget Office on policies for increasing economic growth, dated January
2010, showing that increasing aid to the unemployed has an impact on GDP.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: The second document I am seeking leave to table is  a White House
paper on the Framework Agreement on Middle Class Tax Cuts and Unemployment
Insurance, showing that low-income families are most likely to spend additional money
that they receive in creating jobs and helping growth, dated 7 December 2010.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
15912 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010
Work and Income—Changes to Unemployment Assistance
4. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development and Employment
items.text: What recent changes have been made by Work and
Income for people on unemployment benefits?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.role: Minister for So cial Development and Employment

items.text: We have changed the way Work and Income case management works by letting people
on the unemployment benefit access the firs t available case manager for standard
inquiries. Work and Income has reduced wait ing times and allowed case managers to
see 32 percent more beneficiaries. This is ju st one example of how we are helping more
people into work.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Does she stand by her statements that those who are looking for
work but cannot find it will not be penalised and that she is taki ng great care to be
reasonable in implementing the new work-test requirements; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes, and I have obligations and incentives in place that I
think make it a fairer system. There are obligations on people on the unemployment
benefit to make sure they turn up to appointments and to make sure they are work-ready
wherever possible.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is it reasonable to require a recently unemployed person to seek
at least three job interviews per day in order to comply with the new work-test
requirements or else have their benefit cut,  particularly in places like South Auckland
where there is high unemployment and few jobs available?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The difference is that I believe that people can find work.
I support them in that and back them to get out there an d to go to interviews. I am very
optimistic that they can find work if they are looking.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I do not believe that that
answer addressed the questi on put down by the deputy leader  of the Labour Party. It
was a specific question about the reasonablenes s of the requirement for three interviews
a day. The Minister said she believed in people finding work—I do not think there is
any member of Parliament who does not—s o her answer did not add anything to the
question asked by Annette King.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question asked whether she thought the requirement was
reasonable. That is asking for an opinion, an d there is no precise answer to that. The
Minister’s answer clearly implied—and co rrect me if I am wrong here—that she
thought it was reasonable, or she would have said it was not reasonable. The Minister’s
answer clearly implied that, and if that is not the case she had better correct the answer.
She does not appear to wish to.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is it reasonable to require a recently unemployed person to
apply for 10 jobs—that is, put in 10 app lications a week—otherwise have their
unemployment benefit cut, even if they do no t have the qualifica tions and experience
for those jobs; or does, for example, a 22-year-old unemployed person with no
qualifications applying for a job as professor of maths at Auckland University meet her
work-test criteria?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I say to the member that pe ople cannot find a job unless
they are looking. I support thos e people to look for work. I am quite pleased that Work
and Income is showing them jobs that are available and suggesting they apply. I am sure
that a level of reasonableness is expected  and that people apply for jobs they are
qualified for. The odd mistake may be made , but people cannot find a job unless they
are looking, and that is a key policy for this Government.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What is fair about a situati on where som e people have to
comply with unrealistic obligations for the Minister’s work-test requirements, yet in
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15913
other cases a Minister can go overseas for 6 weeks on full pay and fail to meet her
obligations as a Minister, such  as responding to the Speaker’s request to answer written
questions?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I will tell members what is not reasonable. It is not
reasonable to leave people to a lifetime on th e unemployment benefit and not work test
them, which is what happened for 9 long y ears under the previous Government. This
Government will stand up and put people into work wherever possible. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not know whether the member could hear the answer.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I could not hear a word—but she was showing off anyway.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is my fault that that happen ed. I say to members that there is
nothing wrong with showing support for an an swer, but the level of interjection was
totally unreasonable there, and it is not fair on the person asking the question. Under the
circumstances I am prepared to give the me mber another supplementary question if she
would like to have it. Members have to rea lise that the House deserves to hear an
answer. If the Hon Annette King would like to ask an extra question, the Speaker has
just said that she can.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Do I take from the Minister’s answer that she believes it is
reasonable for a person to apply for a job they have no hope of getting—for example, as
professor of maths at Auckland University when they have no qualification—because it
meets her work-test requirements and therefore makes it right?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No. What she can take from my answer is that we think it
is reasonable that people look for work, that we think it is unreasonable to leave them to
a lifetime of benefit dependency, and that, yes, Work and Income will be case-managing
and working alongside those people who are on the unemployment benefit. I learnt a lot
on my trip away—I thank the member for asking—to the point where I got to have
lunch with her former Prime Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The final supplementary ques tion that was asked by the Hon
Annette King did not contain anything about the member’s trip or lunch appointments.
What is more, the Minister will resume her seat when the Speaker gets to his feet.

items.speaker: Katrina Shanks
items.text: What has been the effect of the Government’s unrelenting focus on
work for young people?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The proportion of young—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There is no way I could hear what the Minister was saying then, at
all. I ask, please, for a little more reasonableness in the House.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The proportion of young people on the unemployment
benefit continues to decrease. It is now at about 30.3 percent of the total. That is down
from 32.1 percent this time last year, and it represents a drop of 736 young people in the
last month. That is great news, no matter which side of the House one sits on.

items.speaker: Hon Jim Anderton
items.text: Can I ask the Minister to be very clear about what she said. As I
understand it, she is saying that all people who are unemployed are looking for work or
are not looking for work—or that all the people who are unemployed and have looked
for work have got a job because they looked. Is that what she is saying?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I can understand that that member might be looking for
work, and I wish him well in that.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It cannot be in order for a
Minister to begin an answer with such a gratuitous put-down of the member asking the
question, particularly a member as senior as—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Som e other members will be leaving this Chamber soon if the place
does not come to order. Members know I am pr etty tolerant of a robust session; there is
no problem with that. But the House is being unreasonable today, and I will not tolerate
that. The Hon Darren Hughes has raised a poi nt of order about the answer that was
15914 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010
given, but had he listened to the supposed question, he would see that as Speaker I
could have ruled the question out of order, be cause it was not really a question at all. It
is very difficult for me to clamp down on a Minister faced with a statement that was
masquerading as a question. I think there has to  be balance in thes e things. With that
kind of question, I cannot be too hard on Minist ers. But I ask the Minister to please not
be gratuitous in answering the question.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I suppose the policy is qu ite clear that people on the
unemployment benefit should be work-ready,  should be able to attend interviews
wherever possible, and should be able to make  themselves as available for work as they
can, as the circumstances arise.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Is the implication of what the Mini ster is saying that the threefold
increase in unemployment beneficiaries und er her watch is because people are not
trying hard enough; if so, how does she ex plain the fact that  2,700 people in my
electorate were looking for 150 jobs at a new supermarket that opened?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, not at all. In  fact, I am pleased  to say that 2,250
people came off the unemployment benefit last month. I believe, though, that there
needed to be a balance of incentives and ob ligations for people, and that is what we
have done.

items.speaker: Rahui Katene
items.text: Does she agree with—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to the member. I ask the Hon Darren Hughes and
Chester Borrows to please stop this interjection exchange across the House. It is totally
discourteous to the member whom I have called to ask her supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rahui Katene
items.text: Does the Minister agree with Mini stry of Social Development chief
executive Peter Hughes, who suggested that the most recent statistics will show a
marked reduction in unemployment benefits an d that half of the placements Work and
Income New Zealand is making are with youn g people; and what place has Community
Max played in such improved outcomes?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes. The Community Max programme has played an
important role in keeping young people attach ed to the workforce during this recession,
especially in our rural communities. Ho wever, long-term outcomes for young people
depend on getting jobs, and as the economy grow s out of this recessi on, our priority is
to get them into work.
Broadband Roll-out—Progress
5. LOUISE UPSTON (National—Taup ō) to the Minister for Communications
and Information Technology : What further progress has been made on rolling out
faster broadband around New Zealand?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): Further to yesterday’s announcement of the first partners of the Ultra-fast
Broadband Initiative, this morning I announced  the short-listing of tenderers for the
Rural Broadband Initiative. This follows quickly on yesterday’s announcement of the
partners that will help to roll out ultr a-fast broadband around Northland and through
cities and towns in the central North Island.  The rural initiative received a number of
high-quality bids, and three have now been placed on a short list. I expect the final
partner to be announced early next year.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What are the economic impacts of the broadband roll-out?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Delivering much faster broadband will greatly improve
telecommunications, lift productivity, and provide for faster growth in New Zealand
relative to that of the rest of the world. Of more immediate benefit, the two deals
announced yesterday will directly lead to th e creation of an estim ated 300 jobs across
the ultra-fast fibre roll-out in Taranaki , Waikato, and the Bay of Plenty, and the
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15915
Northpower roll-out will see an extra 50  people employed. In addition, the Rural
Broadband Initiative will see hundreds more people being employed in developing and
deploying the network to rural schools and communities.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Is it the Government’s intention th at legislation for a regulation-free
period until the end of 2019 for successful bidders will apply to the Rural Broadband
Initiative as well as to the ultra-fast broa dband scheme; if so, w ill that regulation-free
period apply only to new fibre or  to other technologies that have not been laid yet and
that are agreed to in those schemes?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Firstly, I do not agree with the member that it is a
regulation-free period, at all. The pricing will be set by contract between Crown Fibre
Holdings and the bidders for the ultra- fast broadband. The rural broadband will be
different. It will not have the same regulator y mechanism as the ultra-fast broadband, as
it also differs from it in a number of other ways.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What feedback has the Minister received on yesterday’s broadband
announcement?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yesterday’s kick-off of th e urban broadband roll-out
generated some excellent feedback, including from the local councils in the coverage
areas, which universally welcomed the announ cement. In addition, InternetNZ stated:
“Ultra-fast broadband is a game changer” and “The services will be affordable and
really will drive uptake of fibre”. Even IDC analyst Rosalie Nelson said “it is
encouraging to see the emphasis that is bein g placed in the two regions on making fibre
accessible and affordable.”

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: And what did Rod Oram say?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Rod Oram said nothing. The combined urban and rural
initiatives mean we are now on the way to wards ensuring that New Zealand is well
equipped for the future.
Health Services—Taihape
6. Hon RUTH DYSON (Labour—Port Hills)  to the Minister of Health : Will he
act to prevent the closure of health services in Taihape?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As was said yesterday, the Whanganui
District Health Board has acted to prevent th e closure of a large number of services in
Taihape as a result of the trustees deciding to put the Ōtaihape Health Trust into
liquidation. The district health board will he lp retain the genera l practice services,
primary maternity services, day services fo r older people, home-based support services,
radiology services, specialist outpatient serv ices, palliative care services, the mobile
surgical bus, and more. I am keeping in close contact with the district health board as it
works to get the best possible outcome for the people of Taihape.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Why does he think it is OK to force Taihape people aged in their
80s and 90s to move out of their home in th e community they have lived in for years,
and live somewhere else not of their choosing?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Well, of course it is always a very concerning time when a
provider cannot carry on and ther e is uncertainty. What is important is the fact that the
district health board is making arrangeme nts to support those families who may be
affected, but what is clear is that with the liquidation, changes had to be made in
Taihape, and the district health board is working to do that.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Has he picked up the phone to explain to Mrs Wendy Campbell
that having health services closer to home  actually m eans in her home, when she picks
up her 94-year-old mother, Joan, and 96-year-o ld father, Les, from Ruanui House in
Taihape this Saturday?
15916 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Of course, no one is happy that people’s lives are disrupted in
this way. But the fact is the trust has gone into liquidation and the public health service
is doing its level best to make sure that we can maintain as many of those services as the
trust was providing.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Does he think the community w ill notice “very little difference”,
as Simon Power, the current member of Parliament, claimed in a letter, and is that why
the people of Taihape and the district have been pleading for the Government’s help and
finally protesting outside this Parliament because there has been no help from Simon
Power or the Minister, and they know se rvices are being removed from their
community, and staff are losing their jobs?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The real priority here is to make sure that we can secure as
many services for the people of Taihape as the trust was providing. The fact is that the
member opposite has been making claims about  what services may or may not happen
in Taihape when she says that one thing will not be provided, when we know quite
clearly it will be provided. So I would rather rely on what the Whanganui District
Health Board is actually going to provide than what that member chooses to make up.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Does he care that family members will from this Sunday have to
travel for up to 2 hours each way in order to  visit the older fam ily members who have
been, up until now, living in their own community; if he does care, when will he act?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: No one wants older people having their arrangements
disrupted. But the fact is the trust has gone into liquidation, despite  the fact that the
district health board was trying to put in another $1 million worth of services and in-
kind support. A number of those residents are being moved to another rest home. Some,
in fact, are getting closer to their family members.
Bowel Cancer Screening—Pilot Programme
7. Dr JACKIE BLUE (National)  to the Minister of Health : What progress has
been made regarding the 4-year, $24 milli on bowel cancer screening pilot announced in
this year’s budget?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: After years of no progress, yesterday
this Government announced that the Waitematā District Health Board has been selected
to run the 4-year bowel cancer screening pilo t. It is international best practice to
foolproof new screening programmes with a pilot. The Waitemat ā board was chosen
because of its strong focus on screening and its  commitment to working closely with its
neighbouring district health bo ards, primary care, and the No rthern Cancer Network to
ensure that as many people as possible participate in the pilot. Up to 130,000 people
aged 50 to 74 who live in the Waitematā  District Health Board area will be invited to
participate.

items.speaker: Dr Jackie Blue
items.text: What is being done to support th e health sector to deliver the
services that support detection and treatment of bowel cancer?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The member is quite right to identify the need to support the
services that underpin a scr eening programme. That is why I can advise the House that
in the last year nearly 38,000 New Zealande rs had colonoscopies to investigate for
bowel cancer and other serious bowel issues . This was an increase of almost 2,500
colonoscopies over the previous year. These record numbers build on earlier increases
and show that the sector is growing cap acity for this important cancer test. The
Government is fixing public health servic es with a concerted effort to make
colonoscopies more freely and fairly available to New Zealanders who need them .
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15917
New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill—Access to Hearings
8. KEITH LOCKE (Green)  to the Prime Minister : Why is he not supporting
public hearings for submissions on the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service
Amendment Bill?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Up until yesterday the advice I had received
was that such hearings were properly done in  private. However, la st night I received
advice that led me to ask the director of the SIS to reassess th e issue and provide me
with new advice on what the situation should be. I will discuss that advice with the
Intelligence and Security Committee in due course.

items.speaker: Keith Locke
items.text: When the Prime Minister is consider ing that advice, will he take into
account that in February 1999 Prime Minist er Shipley chaired 2 days of public
submissions on a New Zealand Security Intel ligence Service Amendment Bill that even
included a public submission by the former he ad of the British spy agency MI5, Stella
Rimmington?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I will also take into account that Helen Clark in 2001
chaired the GCSB committee in private.

items.speaker: Keith Locke
items.text: Will the Prime Minister also take into account that most committees in
this Parliament have open hearings, but if there is sensitive information, it can be heard
in private or secret, as has happened with the Intelligence and Security Committee in the
past?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, but I am also aware of the advice I have received in the
past, which is that open hearings on this matter,  in relation to this part of the SIS, could
lead to truncated and sterile debate, whic h would not necessarily  lead to a robust
process that we would all want to see.

items.speaker: Keith Locke
items.text: I seek leave to tabl e a couple of documents . I take your ruling, Mr
Speaker, that news media reports are generally not tabled, but in this  case it is not so
much the content of the reports that matter—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What is the source of the document?

items.speaker: Keith Locke
items.text: It is an article by  Guyon Espiner from the Evening Post of 9 February
1999, reporting on a hearing of the Intelligence and Security Committee.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. It is over a decade old. Is
there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Keith Locke
items.text: I seek leave to table an article dated 11 February 1999 from the New
Zealand Herald , showing that the Green Party su bmission by Rod Donald and Keith
Locke was presented in public session to the Intelligence and Security Committee.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is objection.
Police Resourcing—Minister’s Statements
9. Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour—Waimakariri)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Police
items.text: Does she stand by her answer to my  question in the House on 24 November
about whether Deputy Commissi oner Viv Rickard was correct when he confirmed to
the Law and Order Committee that, as at September 2010, the current Government had
contributed just 30 new police officers nationwide since it came into Government, “That
is not, in fact, what Deputy Commissioner Rickard said.”?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I seek leave to table an audio recording from 24 November,
provided to me by an independent m edia organisation—so it is not an uncorrected
transcript from the select committee that ha s not been released—of the police financial
review hearing, which incl udes the comments referred to from Deputy Police
15918 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010
Commissioner Viv Rickard conf irming that the current G overnment had contributed
just 30 new police officers nationwide as at September 2010.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that I have an audio recording of the Law and Order
Committee hearing referred to—which I will make available to the Minister despite the
leave being denied in terms of tabling it, and its being blocked—confirming that Deputy
Police Commissioner Rickard said “Yes”, when  I asked him to confirm that “between
that period June 2009 to September 2010 there is an addition of 30 officers only”, does
she still stand by her answer referred to in my primary question?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: There are several questions th ere, but, yes, I stand by my
original statement, and the reason is that the question the member has just—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: So he’s a liar?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: No, the question the member has just asked is different
from the one he has put down today.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Before I seek leave of
the House, I ask you for your ruling. The pr imary question has to be authenticated by
your office, and the information therein. It was accepted by your office, so therefore it
must be fact and it must be true.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not believe there is anything for me to rule on.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: The Minister denies that that is a fact.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: But as I heard it, the member asked a supplementary question and it
seemed to me that the Minister’s answer  applied to the supplementary question the
member just asked. There is nothing for me to rule on; the Minister replied.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I seek leave, and I will make a detailed description as per
your rulings, to table a transcri pt of the relevant part of the audio recording from the
Law and Order Committee heari ng that confirms that in answer to my question “If we
look at the number of police o fficers as at June 09, not one of those officers was funded
by the current Government, the answer to th at has to be ‘yes’, correct?”, deputy
commissioner Rickard responded “Yes”.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It was a bit unclear from the
start of the member’s leave as to whether the transcripts related to the recording he
referred to earlier that was from an independe nt recording or from the official recording
of the select committee.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I ask the member to clarify that for the House.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Absolutely. They relate to the independent recording that I
have in my possession, not the transcript.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: So long as it is to do with clarification on the document.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, no, not really.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will deal with this. Leave is sought to table that document, is there
any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Given that she claimed in the House on 24 November that
“We have already delivered over 380 pol ice.”, and given deputy commissioner
Rickard’s statement to the Law and Order Committee, can she now explain how many
of her 380 police were funded by the current Government as opposed to the previous
Government?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: As we said in our polic y at the 2008 el ection, 250 police
officers were funded in Budget 2008. That was, in other words, by the previous
Government. We said we would deliver 600 police officers on the front-line by the end
of next year, and that would include the 250. That member is quite wrong in what he
8 Dec 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 15919
said about deputy commissioner Rickard. I suggest that he ge ts his ears checked,
because that was not what he actually said.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much additional funding did this Government provide for
new officers and how many extra officers will be on the front line by the end of 2011?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Good question. In May 2009 this Government injected an
extra $162.4 million of operating funding over 4 years into police recruitment, training,
personnel costs, and deployment. This fundi ng will ensure that we put 600 new officers
on the front line by the end of  next year. We have alrea dy reached our goal of 300 new
officers for Counties-Manukau. It is helping police pilot new polic ing policies, which
are already producing great results. I am sorry that member cannot—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I think the banshee might be—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will just ask his question.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Which is correct: her statement of 24 November that this
Government has “already delivered over 380 police” or de puty commissioner Rickard’s
statements, as verified by the audio I ha ve in my possession and also witnessed by
journalists and reported publicly, recorded on the same day confirming that the National
Government had delivered only 30 police as at September 2010?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: That member is quite incorrect. What we have here are
the correct figures that the police have provided to the select committee. The growth
from the end of November 2008 to the e nd of this month is 384 police officers
delivered; 384 by 30 November.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Will the Minister confirm that Deputy Police
Commissioner Rickard’s honest and straightforward answers to my questions at the
select committee did him no good at all when it came to appointing the new
Commissioner of Police?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: This Government values constabulary independence, and
I have to say it is not something I have seen from Phil Goff and the terrible point-
scoring he has tried to make against the designate commissioner Peter Marshall, a man
of absolute integrity. I can tell him—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I seek leave to make a personal explanation about what the Minister
has just said.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to make a personal explanation about that matter. Is
there any objection to that course of action? There is no objection.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: At no time have I questioned the integrity or the suitability of
Superintendent Marshall, whom I know well and I have worked with. What the Minister
said is absolutely wrong. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The Leader of the
Opposition knows exactly what I am about to say. He cannot accuse a member of being
a liar in the House, and frankly I am surprised that a member such as Mr Goff—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There was such noise in the House that I could not hear what went
on. I can only ask the honourable member whether he accused another member of being
a liar.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I did accuse her of being a liar. I withdraw and apologise, as I must.

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. He has to do it properly. He
knows that that was not the right way to do it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: One of the difficulties is when  there is background noise and I
cannot hear exactly what members are saying.  I did not hear the last words that the
Leader of the Opposition said. It m akes it very difficult for me when I cannot hear what
is being said. The Leader of the Opposition has acknowledged that he did call a member
a liar, and I ask him simply to get to his f eet to withdraw and a pologise, with no other
words.
15920 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I withdraw and apologise . I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. Is it
in order when a member makes a personal explanation to correct another member who
has said something that is wrong, for that member then to carry on, as she did from her
seat, which provoked my response?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We will not take this any further. The member makes an absolutely
fair point. I am on my feet. Members do not make comment when a member is granted
leave to make a personal explanation. That is the end of the matter. What, I must say,
led to this period of disorder was a question that perhaps I should have ruled out of
order, but I did not. It was my fault, because it certainly led to th e disorder I expected
when the question was asked. The member knows who asked the question. The member
should not look puzzled. Maybe I should have ru led the question out, but that is what
led to the disorder and I think the House should come back to a semblance of order.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I have two points of
order. My first point of orde r is one of consistency, and I ask for your ruling on it. You
required the Leader of the Opposition to withdraw and apologise for a term that was
used that was unparliamentary. You allowed, in a previous questi on, the Minister of
Health to say to my colleague, the opposite number, that she was making it up, which is
tantamount to exactly the same thing, and you let that fly. I ask fo r your ruling on that,
first.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Let me deal with that. I invite the member to go back and look at
the Hansard of the question asked by his colleag ue. He will find that the member
inserted into the supplementary question a lot of information for which there was no
authentication. A Minister is perfectly at liberty to question the accuracy of such
information in a question. I would ask that Ministers do not do it in  a gratuitous way,
but they are perfectly at liberty to question th e accuracy of such information and that is
what I believe the Minister did. If there is a further point of order, I will listen to it.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: As you are fond of teaching us in this House—and I mean
that in a positive way—and giving us the odd tutorial, which is appreciated—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will just make his point of order.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: What I would like is for you to advise me as to why the
final question I asked, which was simply  whether the Minist er could confirm
something, is out of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I invite the member to go back and look at the Hansard, because he
implied in his question that the Minister had interfered in the appointment of a senior
official because of something said at a sele ct committee. That is verging on the kind of
thing that could be argued to be outrageous and could be ruled out. I did not rule it out,

items.text: Does he share Ngāi Tahu’s concern that the bill “would revisit on us

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member has made a very good point  of order. It is quite correct
that supplementary questions must relate to the Minister’s re sponsibilities, and
questioners need to be careful not to ask about the detail of the bill, which is the
responsibility of the Attorney -General. I invite the member to restate her question,
bearing that in mind. Her primary question wa s perfectly OK, because it asked whether
the Minister stood by his statement and what co ncerns he had raised with the Attorney-
General, but she cannot question the Minister ab out the detail of the bill, because that is
not that Minister’s responsibility.

items.speaker: Hilary Calvert
items.text: It was asking whether he had any concerns about Ngāi Tahu’s—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I invite the member to restate he r question, and I ask for silence so
that I can hear it properly, because it is an important matter.

items.speaker: Hilary Calvert
items.text: Does he share Ngāi Tahu’s concern as stated in the submission they
made to the M āori Affairs Committee that the bill “w ould revisit on us th e injustices of
the past because it is built on tests that ex clude us from our rights, based on past
injustices.”?

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I ask again for your
clarification in respect  of the seeking of an opinion, pa rticularly about the Marine and
Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. The que stion seems to be heading in the same
direction, and therefore should be fairly and squarely in  the hands of the Hon Mr
Finlayson, surely.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is an interesting issue. The question asked whether the Minister
shared the concerns of Ng āi Tahu, who made submissions  on the bill. Ministers,
especially the Minister of M āori Affairs, can be asked for their opinion about matters
affecting Mā ori, without the need for them to comment on the detail of the bill. The
Minister is definitely not responsible for the detail of the bill. I believe that the Minister,
in so far as he is able, give n that he is not responsible for the bill, could attempt to
answer that question.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The problem  might be,
firstly, that the Hon Dr Pita Sharples was not at the select comm ittee hearings and is
unable to offer an opinion on that submission, because he has not seen it. Therefore the

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member has made a perfec tly good point—that would be a
perfectly good answer. That is the thing. In  answering that kind of question, Ministers
who are not responsible for a bill can answer in that way.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Although I am not responsible for the bill, it will come

items.speaker: Hilary Calvert
items.text: Does the Minister of M āori Affairs agree with M āori Party MP

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell

15922 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Dec 2010
must surely fit with the Attorney-General, w ho has responsibility for this particular bill.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: These are important issues, and I would like to suggest that a

items.speaker: Hilary Calvert
items.text: Has the Minister of M āori Affairs received advice concerning any

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I

items.text: It definitely does not. If member s wish to raise questions about the

8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15925

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . Mr Speaker, you regularly offend members of the House,
and I know that you regard it as an important part of your job.
It is happy days in the Labour Party. Trevor Mallard lost his pills, Phil Goff lost his
marbles, the caucus is losing its temper, David Caygill lost his respectable place in
Labour Party history by being mixed up with David Cunliffe, and Kris Faafoi almost
lost the unloseable seat. This is the Labour Party that set out with  the “Axe the Tax”
campaign, and in the Mana by-election it bur ied the axe in its own back. What was
meant to be a referendum on the Government  ended up with the people of middle New
Zealand—and there is no seat more middl e New Zealand than Mana—sending the
Opposition a message. But Phil Goff did not get it. He did not get it, because he decided
that rather than listen to the people of  Mana, he would google the Labour Party in
Britain. He came up with—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sorry to interrupt the

beginning of his speech that made reference to a member having not taken his pills.
That phrase has been ruled out at the re quest of National members, for reasons
reasonably close to home, in that respect. If National members are to object to that
phrase being used by Labour members about one of their members, then I do not think it
is in order for them to use that phrase about  one of our members. We take objection to
the use of that phrase, in order for there to be consistency with regard to the sensitivities
on that point.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member asking that he withdraw—

items.text: It is an unnecessarily gratuitous comment; I fully accept that. I ask
the member to withdraw the comment. I do not think members should be using that
comment.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I withdraw. Well, Labour will need some other explanation
for Trevor’s extraordinary behaviour, which I suggest is that he did not attend his anger
management course the other day.
How did Labour manage to almost lose the Mana by-election? I think the first reason
is that no one is listening to Labour, and the reason that no one is listening to it is that 2
years on from the 2008 election, Labour still thi nks the voters were wrong. It is highly
unlikely that the voters of middle New Zealan d, even in a recession,  would listen to

The second reason is that if voters were to  listen, then what th ey would hear would
not make any sense. I will just use a couple of examples. [ Interruption] Well, that is
why they are saving themselves the trouble, because it would not make any sense. I will
give a couple of examples. David Caygill—so rry, David Cunliffe—has said that he is
against asset sales. He said that Labour’s policy now is that the Government will go into

dilute taxpayers’ ownership.

the Government still owns it, 100 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Socialism.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is modern social democr acy, I think. That is actually
impossible. Labour members need to decide—well, actually, they have decided. They
15926 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
are in favour of partial privatisation. They are. Privatisation dilutes taxpayers’

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How are they going to do that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A very good question. The answer is that it will spend more.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is how Labour will do it. How do we know that? Well,
because it will get rid of GST on food. Apparently, doing that  will not cost anything. It

The other reason we know that Labour will spend more is that it opposes every single

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: $500 million for sleepovers, they have promised.

items.text: Labour has promised $500 million for sleepovers, plus
GST—that is $800 million—plus the $2.5 billion it will borrow to put into the

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: On 17 November 2008
the Prime Minister said: “I expect high standa rds from my Ministers. If they don’t meet
the standards I set, then obviously I will take action if necessary.” It is interesting that
Mr English is the first speaker in this debate from the other side of the House. He talked
at length about what he thi nks New Zealand people believe. I say this to Mr English:
they believe that the Prime Minister has not lived up to the standards he set for himself
and his Ministers. The New Zealand people believed it was not on when Mr English
dodged, weaved, squirmed, and tried everything  he could to get around the rules when
he claimed for a house—I think it was in the order of $24,000. He claimed for a house,
and rented it, through Ministerial Services, back to his trust. I say to that member that
the people of New Zealand believed all too well that he dodged, weaved, behaved
inappropriately, and cheated.
What was the Prime Minister’s response to  that? Was it to admonish him? Was it to
sack him? Was it to censure him? No, it was to change the rules—the ministerial
rules—so that not only could he get $24,000, bu t he and every Minister, I think, could
get in the order of $48,000 or thereabouts with out producing a receipt. He did not get
sacked—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: I seek leave to make a personal explanation relevant to what the
member has just said.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: The member has given the impre ssion that under the new rules I
claim a housing allowance. That is incorrect: I claim no housing allowance.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I endorse his statement, because he does so by
choice. He could still claim th e new housing allowance. If he did it is within the rules.
But because the feet were put to the fire month after month, day after day because of his
dodgy arrangements, he had no option but to say to the Prime Minister that even though
he could claim under the new rules, which the Prime Minister rewrote to benefit him, he
would not do so. That is the part of the explanation we did not hear. What was the new
higher standard there? The rules were changed to suit him.
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15927
Then we had Richard Worth. We will no t go down that track too much. Another
standard was breached. There was another dodgy deal overseas by a member who is
now not in this place. The Prime Minister  stood by Richard Worth day after day, month
after month until the inevitable happened.
Then we come to Rodney Hide, the great perk-buster. The ACT members
“Tweedledumb and Tweedledumber” over there stand up for him every day. He is the
man who railed, destroyed careers, and attacked families because he viewed MPs’ use
of travel allowances as perks and inappropriate. He was then unzipped—I will not say
from where—and was found to be using trav el allowances for his own purposes. That
was the height of—there is a word that you will not let me use, Mr Speaker, and I
accept that. We know what the word is. Wh at was the high standard? What did the
Prime Minister do then? He did nothing.
Then there was strike two on Mr Hide. He  stood by and aided and abetted a former
member who covered up a suppression order. He knew about a former member of this
House who stole a dead child’s identity. What did the Prime Minister do then? He said
that that was in a private capacity and was nothing to do with him.
Then we had Phil Heatley. Do members remember the old limousine or self-drive car
following the train all the way to Nelson so that he could drive back? I do not know
whether it was full of flowers or presents—w ho knows? Then there were the half-dozen
bottles of wine at the National Party conference on the ministerial credit card. What was
the Prime Minister’s response th en? It was to take him out to relax and bring him back.
Where were the high standards and where was the action there?
Then, of course, we had Mr Finlayson—“ Mr Grumpy”, all right—who for 4 years
never declared among his pecuniary interests that he had a directorship. Dame Margaret
Bazley said that that was incorrect and a false return. No action was taken; it was a
mistake!
Then, of course, we come to the doozy: Pansy Wong. I put to members that the
investigation carried out on Pa nsy Wong is a cover-up. It is a cover-up because, to my
knowledge, no one in history who has pleaded guilty to the accusations and said that
funds were misused is then investigated in the following way. She was asked to produce
a few diaries, and asked wh ether she has done it again. The answer was no. She was

of corroborating evidence. That  investigation would not st and up in a court. We know
that a former member of this House was ch arged and found guilty of a similar offence.
But what is the action here? She is out of Cabinet.
The Prime Minister says that if you plead guilty once you are clear ed. It is OK, just
do not plead guilty too many times! That is the higher standard of National and that, I
say to Mr English, is what the New Zealand people believe.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Two years into being in Opposition, in its
second year in Opposition, and Labour is exactly where it was 2 years ago. It is roughly
where it was in the polls. Phil Goff’s ratings are a bout the same as they were. In fact,

Voodoo economic policy has arrived with a couple  of speeches in the last couple of
weeks from the Labour finance spokesman and from the Leader of the Opposition.
Voodoo economics is here. There are flip flops , the “Axe the Tax” bus races around the
country, but there is no commitment. Voodoo taxes are on the way if the Labour Party

though the Crown collects $1.5 million a year  and it costs the economy $70 million.
That is voodoo economics. Voodoo GST changes are coming according to Labour. It

It has a voodoo leader who is now copyi ng and pasting speeches from the United
Kingdom Labour Party. Labour is promoting a voodoo monetary policy. It is actually
doing the exact reverse of what every cen tral bank and every Government around the
world is doing to try to address the global fi nancial crisis. Labour is trying to weaken,

Labour has a voodoo accounting policy now. I bring members a quote from the
person who would like to one day be the next Minister of Fina nce. Just listen to this

only on one side of the Crown’s balance sh eet—“and need not increase net debt, but
does increase net worth.” What on earth is th at about? A third- form economics student
would be failed and sent to the back of the class if they put that kind of stuff in an essay.
I have no idea what it is about. It is voodoo accounting coming from the voodoo Labour
Party. It has a voodoo finance spokesman—we ar e not sure whether it is Mr Caygill
resurrected or Mr Cunliffe, and even Mr Go ff is not too sure. It has a voodoo investing
policy: it wants to borrow from foreign market s to give to the Superannuation Fund to
invest in foreign markets. I cannot work that one out.
The inbound transactions tax is a voodoo tax. That is what Labour is now promoting.
What would it mean? Higher interest rates fo r New Zealand. That is a tax on exports.
Every receipt that comes into New Zeal and under a Labour Government would be
caught up by this new thing called the inbound transactions tax. Any money sent home
by New Zealanders—our kids overseas or friends overseas wanting to send money
home—will be subject to Labour’s new voodoo inbound transactions  tax. I am very,
very fearful of what it might do. Labour essentially wants our kids to stay away and stay
away for longer. Why does it hate success so much?
Labour has a voodoo asset management policy. Labour wants to take a more active
role in the economy. Not one of its members ha s spent more than 5 minutes in the real
sector—not one. Mr Goff wants to put on his shorts, socks, and sandals, get his
clipboard, put his pens in his pocket, and go around various State-owned enterprises and
tell them how to run the show. That is what the new voodoo asset management policy of
the Labour Opposition is promoting. It want s to unleash State-owned enterprises and
their subsidiaries—or not their subsidiaries. Essentially, it wants to sell Kiwibank,
according to a speech from Mr Cunliffe the other day. He forgot, I guess, that Kiwibank
is a subsidiary of New Zealand Post, but subsidiaries are the things that Labour wants to
dilute the equity of.
This National-led Government is doing an awesome job. We have a challenging
economic programme. We are delivering better, smarter public services. We are
reforming regulation, education and skills, and business innovation, and are investing in
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15929
productive infrastructure. This countr y does not need vood oo economics or voodoo
Labour policies.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Today I will talk very briefly about
the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations —talks that have been under way in
Auckland. Most people think that the Trans-Pacific Partnership is about trade; in fact,
very little of it is about trad e. Most of it is about trying  to restrict the ability of
Governments to make regulations.
When we look at some of the issues that  are on the table in the negotiations around
the Trans-Pacific Partnership, we see that they are issues like restricting the ability to
control foreign investment. When Australia negotiated its trade deal with the United
States, it gave away the righ t to have any restrictions on  incoming investment from the
United States into Australia up to a level of A$800 million, which effectively gutted
Australia’s entire foreign investment review process for US investment. That is one of
the issues that the United States has put on the table.
A second issue it has put on the table is our GE food labelling laws. Biotech
companies in the United States do not like our GE food labelling laws, or the Australian
ones, and they are trying to get them removed as part of the trade negotiations.
Another part of the negotiations that I think is critically important is the investor-
State disputes mechanism. As part of these free-trade deals, a disputes mechanism is
established whereby corporations can sue Governments in international tribunals. These
tribunals are generally set up at the World Bank. They are th ree-person tribunals that
make binding decisions on Governments. These tribunals have in the past required
Canada to allow a toxic additi ve into its petrol. Canada tried to remove a toxic additive
from its petrol, but was sued by Ethyl Corporation, which was the producer. Ethyl
Corporation argued that Canada had expr opriated Ethyl Corporation by banning the
toxic additive, and it was able to win its case.
Recently, Argentina lost a case when it tried to intervene to protect water supply.
Argentina argued that it had to intervene b ecause water is a basic human necessity. The
tribunal established at the World Bank said  that just because something was a human
right did not mean that it ove rrode trade rules. Trade ru les actually trump the human
right to water.
Labour and National are very keen for us to sign up to these agreements. Investor-
State disputes resolution pr ovisions were in the New Zealand - China free-trade
