agreement that the former Labour Government  negotiated. These kinds of issues are on
the table.
How does the New Zealand public find out wh at is part of these negotiations? We
know that the New Zealand Government ha s produced a series of position papers
outlining the position of the New Zealand Gove rnment, and they have been given to all
the other negotiating countries. For example, the Sultan of Brunei knows what the New
Zealand Government’s position is on, let us say, intellectual property. But the New
Zealand people do not know what the Ne w Zealand Government’s position is on
intellectual property, because the New Zeal and Government has not released the
position papers that it has given to the other negotiating parties.
When we asked the Government about this , it said it could not release the position
papers, because it would undermine our negotiating position. That is not a rational
argument. The other countries already know New Zealand’s negotiating position
because we have given them the position pa pers outlining our negotiating position. The
only people who do not know New Zealand’ s negotiating position are the people of
New Zealand. The other countries are entirely aware of our negotiating position because
we have given them our position papers. It is a matter of public record that our
15930 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
Government has presented these position pa pers to the other Governments in the
negotiations, but has not publicly released them.
The Government cannot argue that it would undermine the negotiating strategy when
New Zealand’s position is already known to the other negotiating parties. How can it be
right that the New Zealand public is not to ld what New Zealand is telling the other
Governments in these negotiations? There needs to be greater transparency so that we,
the public—and even members of this Parliament—have a right to see what New
Zealand is telling the other parties to the negotiations.
I argue that the reason the New Zealand public is not being told is that what the New
Zealand Government is offering would be very unpopular. If the New Zealand
Government was offering to establish inve stor-State disputes mechanisms whereby
other corporations can sue our Government in international tribunals, that would be very
unpopular amongst the New Zealand public. If the New Zealand Government was
offering to get rid of our GE food labelli ng laws, that would be very unpopular. If the
New Zealand Government was offering to get ri d of our investment rules, that would be
very unpopular. That is why the Government is not releasing the position papers to the
New Zealand public. It should. These negotiations need transparency.

items.speaker: CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: How comfortable it must be on
the other side of the House to be in Opposition, to make all the promises those members
want to make, and to never have to address the question of where the money will be
found. This morning on Radio New Zealand we  heard the Leader of the Opposition
complain about money not being put into the so-called Cullen fund, obviously implying
that a Labour Government would put money in to that fund if it happened to have the
privilege of being in Government right now, but he never explained where it would find
that money. Labour has taken slap after slap, yet it never ever has to cough up. That is
the privilege of being in Opposition: those members can stand there and pick whatever
fights they want to take on; they can promise everything, k nowing they will never have
to deliver; and before they would ever have to deliver anything, they will remove it. We
saw them all on the bus singing “Take Me  Home, Country Roads”, longing for the
fatherland, etc.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: “Slip Sliding Away”, I think.

items.speaker: CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Sliding around in that big red bus that said “Axe the Tax”.
Funnily enough, tax seems to have gone off the agenda at the moment. In spite of all the
promises about no GST on fresh fruit and vege tables, Labour is not saying what it
would do with the 15 percent GST. It is not  making any comment about it whatsoever.
It is strangely silent right now.
Labour knows that it has to keep its consti tuents disgruntled and disenchanted—that
is code for poor and pissed off—so that it can maintain a constitu ency come the next
election. When we look at the smacks Labour members had around the House today in
question time—for instance, having a go at good old Paula Bennett—we heard them
saying: “There are no jobs, there are no jobs.” In fact, Labour criticised the Minister for
Social Development and Employment for exp ecting people to make  applications for
jobs so they continue receiving an unemployment benefit. Is that not what a Minister for
Social Development and Employment is supposed to do? Is it shallow to just stand back
and say: “There are no jobs, there are no j obs.”? Would we not expect a person with
their hand out in receipt of a benefit from th e taxpayers of New Zealand to at least be
trying to look for work? Th en we had the Leader of the Opposition stand up and
complain to the Minister for Social De velop ment and Employment because of a
situation where 2,500 people who are unemployed wanted to a pply for a job, as if that
was some terrible thing. National believes that people should be trying to look for work,
and so did those 2,500 people who were in that queue looking for work.
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15931
Those people are actually on our side and they are actually supporting what we are
saying, just as people in Ma na did a couple of weeks ago. Phil Goff stood up and said
that that by-election would be  run on the Government’s performance, and we agreed.
We put our record on the line, and we know  that Labour got an absolute caning in
Mana. Its 6,300 vote majority in that electorate at the last election went through the
floor to 1,080 on the night and ended up at about 1,400.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Mana said “Hell no!” to Hekia.

items.speaker: CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Carmel Sepuloni knows exactly that, and she hates it. The
fact is that the Prime Minister, John Key, is the most popular Prime Minister since
Adam was a cowboy, and Labour hates it. The public of New Zealand is repeating time
and time again that it is happy with the perf ormance of this Government. Even in a
pretty crappy week, the public is prepared to cut us some slack. Given the terrible times
that this Government has had to endure a nd defend in order to support the country of
New Zealand, the public of New Zealand is prepared to give us the benefit of the doubt
and cut us some slack because they know better than anything else that they do not want
that lot back any time soon.

items.speaker: RAHUI KATENE
items.text: Today is a really auspicious day
for the Māori Party. It is an auspicious day for M āori and it is an auspicious day for the
country. I am really disappointed that none of the other speakers in this debate so far
have even mentioned the fact  that this morning our co -leader Pita Sharples stood
alongside the Deputy Prime Minister and announ ced a new phase of public debate to be
generated around New Zealand’s constitutional arrangements.
This is the day we have been leading up to since the agreement was signed with
National, and we note that other political parties said they have been looking towards
this day, asking that they be part of this debate. Well, today is it. This is the day when
our constitutional review is starting, and it is a fantastic day.
In his book The Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand’s Law and Constitution ,
Matthew Palmer expresses his view that Te Tiriti o Waitangi contributes greatly to the
objective of healthy relations hips between the Crown, M āori, and other New
Zealanders. Mr Palmer concludes that in order to better achieve that objective, change is
desirable. Change is good—change that stabilis es the place of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in
New Zealand’s law and constitution. Today the drive to stabilise the place of the Treaty
of Waitangi in New Zealand’s law and constitution enters new terrain.
I wish that other members of  the House were as excited as our party is about this,
because this is the day that we have been  looking forward to for so long and that M āori
have been working towards for decades. As a first-term MP and a lawyer by trade and
by inclination, it is almost beyond my wildest dreams that in such a short time we, the
Māori Party, have been able to place the constitutional significance of Te Tiriti o
Waitangi firmly on the agenda.
The second anniversary of my maiden statement in this Parliament is just days away.
In that speech I referred to the many hours I had spent in the C ourt of Appeal being
educated in the practice and impact of c onstitutional law. I will remind members of the
challenge this Parliament has until now failed to live up to. I am referring, of course, to
the ruling of the Court of Appeal in New Zealand Maori Council v Attorney-General. In
his summary the President of the Court of Appeal, Sir Robin Cooke, stated: “We have
reached two major conclusions. First, that the  principles of the Treaty of Waitangi
overrides everything else in the State Own ed Enterprises Act. Second, that those
principles require the Pakeha  and Maori partners to act towards each other reasonably
and with the utmost good faith.”
Those words are pivotal in  our pathway to nationhood. Fo r too long our nation has
suffered the injustice of being one of only thr ee countries in the entire world to have no
15932 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
written constitution. We are one of three in the whole world with no written
constitution. Commentators refer to a veritable patchwork quilt of significant
legislation, several legal documents, comm on law derived from court decisions, and
established constitutional practices known as conventions.
A vital thread running through all these documen ts has been the status of Te Tiriti o
Waitangi as a founding document of government in New Zealand. Today in this House
we appreciate that article 1 of the Treaty is in itself the basis for the current government
structures in New Zealand, expressing the ri ght of the Crown to govern. We know that
article 2 of the Treaty guarantees to Mā ori te tino rangatiratanga over our lands, estates,
forests, fisheries, and taonga—the full, excl usive, and undisturbed possession of all that
we treasure as the ultimate expression of our identity. Article 3 of the Treaty affirms the
equal citizenship rights of all New Zealanders, including M āori. Article 3 also promises
the Queen’s royal protection to M āori. A measure of this pr otection would be the well-
being of Māori.
Such a rudimentary summary of ideals and aspirations emerging from our foundation
document, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, is not, regr ettably, something that  all New Zealanders
feel equipped to express. Surveys have been carried out over the years. One survey that
was carried out 5 years ago by UMR Research found that levels of awareness varied: 71
percent of Māori are aware of the document, but only 51 percent of Pākehā are aware of
it. This needs to change. It will change through this constitutional review. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: It is clear that the Government is on a slide in
terms of its popularity with the voters of New Zealand. That is now abundantly clear.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Here we go—National memb ers continue to deny the
reality of the numbers. The trend has been clear for 2 years. In fairness, in 18 months
the gap is narrowing, and narrowing substa ntially. Phil Heatley is cackling in the
background like he has completely lost the plot.
Actually, the first person to pick the signi ficance of the narrowing gap was a former
employee of the National Party. It was a former employee of the Speaker, Matthew
Hooton. Matthew Hooton picked this about a year ago. He said that the gap was
narrowing and that National should not rest on its laurels. But it has.
The latest poll, which is of most concern to the National Party, was on the front page
of the Sunday Star-Times on the weekend. It had Nationa l on 34 percent and Labour on
28 percent—a 6 percent gap. It is now a 6 percent gap, whereas a year and a half ago it
was a 20 percent gap. It is down from 20 percent to 6 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: And who’s got the 6 points?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Winston Peters fills that gap at the moment, together with
the Greens. But a two-party swing of onl y 3 percent would see Labour ahead of
National. No wonder National is starting to get worried. Those members are getting so
worried, what do they do in respect of thes e polls? The first thing that politicians who
are worried about polls do is rubbish them. What happened here? The headline is “Key
rubbishes NZ First results”.
Those m
embers are so worried about Winston Peters. He turned up to the Mā ori
Affairs Committee today and panned their legislation on the foreshore and seabed. I ask
whether members can guess how many questions the National majority asked of
Winston Peters at the select committee, despite  his strident criticism of what they are
doing. How many?

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: A dozen or so?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: No, less. How many?

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Five?
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15933

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: None. They did not have the courage to take on the Rt Hon
Winston Peters with even one question at the select committee in support of their bill.
What lies behind the slide of popularity for National is people’s concern about a lack
of integrity. That integrity has two aspects to it. The first is personal integrity. People
are disappointed in the Hon Phil Heatley, in Bill English, and in Pansy Wong. Overall,
they are disappointed with the lack of standards enforced by the Prime Minister,
notwithstanding that he promised to hold higher standards than his predecessors. People
are disappointed with the lack of integrity ar ound ministerial performance, but also they
are disappointed with broken promises. They have stopped trusting National. There has
been broken promise after broken promise. National said it would not increase GST, but
it did. National members said they would not increase GST, but they did. They said they
would bridge the wage gap with Australia—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Oh, they’ve given up on that.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: —and they have given up on that. Their rhetoric on that has
disappeared. They were going to close the wage gap by 2025. They had all sorts of
weird and wonderful plans that they said would do it, like mining in national parks,
which they abandoned.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: A cycleway.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: A cycleway would not make much difference. They have
no credible plan. They will not even ag ree on milestones between now and 2025, which
is their target date. We all know that the gap is growing larger rather than narrowing.
Another area of failed polic y is in respect of  the major settings of the economy.
National said it would not borrow for tax cuts ; it borrowed for tax cuts. The amount of
that borrowing is increasing by the month. In the last quarter  alone the Government has
had to acknowledge an extra $2 billion of Government deficit—that is, cumulatively,
New Zealanders owe $2 billion more to overseas banks through the Government’s
indebtedness than was predicted by the Government in its Budget. Why? It was in part
to fund tax cuts, 42 percent of which went to  the top 10 percent of income earners. That
is another broken promise by National. It prom ised a fair tax system, not a tax system
that delivered the majority of tax cuts to those who already earn the most.
That is why the Government’s popularity is sliding. That is why the two-party gap is
less than 6.5 percent.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: It was the weeks leading up to Christmas and all
through Welling-town,
Not a Labour MP was happy; they all had a big frown,
Conditions in the Labour Party were all looking so sullen,
Calls were made out of Te Atatū to call back “Auntie Helen”.
With Phil in a mess, not knowing where to turn, he has even decided to recite a fable,
And bring back in the finance role a dinosaur called Caygill.
It was no surprise, given the announcement of their plans to float off SOEs, bring
back free fishing classes, and GST-free rates for fruit,
Pity no one in Labour has thought about how to pay for it.
Labour is working on the economic theory of pixies at the bottom of the garden,
While National’s numbers continue to harden.
“No worries, Labour’s plan will work.” says Nash with a grin. Everyone in Labour
smiles inanely,
Despite no one in caucus understanding how to calculate GST, even badly.
“Do not worry, Andrew Little has a plan. He holds his tarot cards closely, which only
goes to show
Labour has no idea in 2011 where it should go.
You see, David Cunliffe suffers from a split personality;
15934 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
The public do not believe he has a solution for their malady.
But still daily he stands on a platform, preaching with gusto, and preens like a proud
peacock with a chest full of puff,
But when questioned on his economic voodoo, it is all a load of fluff.
Cunliffe does not know his Krugman from his Samuelson,
But “Don’t panic!” thinks Goff; “We will bring back Labour’s son
Caygill, deep from the past. He’ll solve it, I am sure.”, Phil crows. Meanwhile the
economy slowly and surely continues under National, and grows.
Labour—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Did Cam Calder write this speech?

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: It gets better, I tell Mr Hughes.
Labour stands and promises that the world is flat and simple like some tricky game
of monopoly,
But the socialists’ policy, puffery, and PR will not solve the economy.
“Spend more on the masses!”, the left squeals;
“Billions of dollars are required.”, they say. Shower billions on the poor for the
wounds of the 90s to heal.
“Soak the rich!” says Labour, “They have plenty.”
Ignoring the fact under Labour the middle class’s piggy banks were all empty.
It seems Mr Cunliffe has forgotten his te am, 9 years in charge, are responsible for
our being in recession
So much so there has been a procession
Of experts and advisers telling New Zealand “Save more! You must change!”.
But Labour is like an ostric h with its head in the sand;  everyone who does not agree
with them is just a capitalist and strange.
The year 2010, to be fair, has not been the best,
With earthquakes ruining my home town of  Christchurch, plane crashes, and mine
disasters—lest we forget.
But the people of New Zealand are wise and they are smart,
Because 2 years ago they elected a Key G overnment, which has delivered and given
them a pleasant surprise.
John Key has provided them with economic leadership,
The economy is growing money in people’s back pockets, and they continue to enjoy
healthy fellowship.
With our programme of infrastructure  investment, innova tion, smarter public
services, education standards, and tax reform,
The voters understand it, and the Labour Party sits there looking forlorn.
With seemingly the wisdom of Charlie’s Angels on our team,
Good ideas and the confidence of the peop le of New Zealand keep flowing to
National in a rapid stream.
So come Cunliffe, come Parker, come Mallard and King, come Hughes and come
Goff,
The public thinks they have no economic idea and just want to switch them off.
As their policies are all voodoo, and their people are leaving in masses,
Bring on election 2011, as our John Key - le d Government will leave them all in
tatters.

items.speaker: Hon PETE HODGSON
items.text: Aaron Gilmore has just given
us verse, not cleverly done and certainly no t terse. The joke is on him, for today’s
speaking list are Cabinet wannabes who regrettably missed.
The Prime Minister must refer the Pansy Wong issue to the Auditor-General for
investigation, and must do so soon. That is what the Prime Minister did with Phil
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15935
Heatley, it is what happened in the case of Bill English—after a period of delay, I
acknowledge—and it should happen in the case of Pansy Wong. Should the Prime
Minister do that, an investigation into an area of possible misuse of public moneys can
be conducted by an office that is  respected and exists to look  into the use and misuse of
public moneys.
That is why we have an Aud itor-General’s office. It is an office capable of measured
judgments. In the case of Phil Heatley, for example, it was capable of giving him a rapid
re-entry straight back into Cabinet. In the case of Pans y Wong, that door was closed by
the appointment earlier this week of Hekia Parata. But it  does not close the door for
ever.
Indeed, I think Pansy Wong would welcome an investigation for a couple of different
reasons. The first is that she might find herself getting the Phil Heatley treatment, where
the matter was found to be minor. No instances beyond it were found in the McPhail
report. There was nothing more to discover. It was a $500 job. The money has been paid
back. It was not deliberate, systemic, systematic, or anything like that. That is a
possibility.
Another reason she might be pleased for the Auditor-General to look at her case is
that the information flow to us—certain ly, to me—will stop. It stopped when the
McPhail report got under way. For 2 or 3 week s, the information that had been flowing
in to me and that I had been putting into  the public arena as it came to pass stopped. I
stopped putting anything into the public arena; there was nothing to put in.
On Friday the McPhail report came out, a nd it was panned by Friday evening as
being an inadequate report. It does not mean that it is wron g, but it does not draw a line
under the case, because it does not have credib ility. There is no signi ficant certainty of
its being right—so say the media, and so sa y I. I do not think it is a thorough report. So,
of course, as Friday evening turned into the weekend, the information started to flow
again. It just comes, and it is time-consumi ng. Much of it has to be translated from
Mandarin. I continue to put it in the public arena, as I ha ve done today, and I may well
do tomorrow. Who knows? I may well do it next week. Again, who knows? Pansy
Wong has to put up with that, and I do not think it is fair on her.
Of course, I could stop, but I am not going to, because my job and my duty—there is
no need to grin about it, Mr Assistant Speaker Roy—is to hold the Government to
account. That is the job of Her Majest y’s loyal Opposition. People can call me a
muckraker, but that is the reason why the We stminster system is set up as it is. I will
continue to put this information into the public arena, as long as I can prove using
written evidence that it is true. I get an awful lot of rumour, which does not go any
further, because I do not know whether it is true. But when I can show that something is
true or very likely to be true, I will put it into the public arena. I will continue to do so.
It is not good for Pansy Wong. I think sh e would want it stopped, and I think the
Prime Minister can stop it by taking her case an d ringing up the Auditor-General and
asking, just like with the Phil Heatley case, that she please look at it.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Sitting here and listening to some of the members of
the Opposition talking about higher moral grounds reminds me of a time when the
previous Labour Government was in power, and David Parker was quoted as saying
something about the higher standards of th e Prime Minister’s predecessor. I just
mention Taito Phillip Field and “paintergate”. I  also say that at least our Prime Minister,
John Key, paints his own pictures . Mr Parker—or is he Mr Ca ygill or Mr Cunliffe, as I
cannot remember—must have polled his own lounge room, because that is the only way
he would get that kind of a result. Money does not grow on trees and cannot be found at
the bottom of the garden where pixies live , but that is exactly what Labour members
seem to believe. Or maybe they believe that the fairy godmother will return to give them
15936 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
some ideas on how they will finance their policies, as they certainly do not seem to have
any answers.
Their leader, Mr Goff, talked about lo wering GST at the cost of $3 billion—not $3
million; $3 billion. The finance spokespers on, Mr Cunliffe—or shall I call him Mr
Caygill—promised that Labour will not go on a spending binge. It would be good to
know how Labour would conjure up the extra money—and that is exactly what it will
be doing: conjuring. Labour’s financial manage ment, or rather mismanagement, has left
us facing a decade of deficits. It was hopi ng for some magic to get us through these
difficult times, but the New Zealand public saw through the magic tricks and wanted the
safe and sound economic management of a National Government to get us out of the rut
and to move this country forward.
I ask about Labour’s promise to use KiwiSaver to help Kiwis save more without
increasing the squeeze on their income today. Who will pay for that? It is probably the
same story from that side of the House: “Jus t slap it on the bill, Mr Phil Goff.” Maybe
Mr Goff mistaking Mr Cunliffe for Mr Ca ygill speaks louder about the inner workings
of Mr Goff’s mind. Perhaps he is yearning for the old days when Labour privatised
everything, or perhaps it is a reaction to the undermining nature of the factional
currents, which are apparently strong curren ts. Did we not hear a bout the 17 friends of
the Te Atatū member, Chris Carter, who were working against—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: I think there are more now.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Are there more now? Maybe that is the problem—strong currents
for a leadership coup, but maybe the prince is not quite ready to rock the boat just yet.
Another magic show that Labour is relyi ng on is that the New Zealand public will
forget that savings fell under the long 9 years of the La bour Government. Inflation
soared, spending increased, and many Kiwis left New Zealand. It is not a good sign
when Kiwis leave our country, when they do not want to be Kiwis and they want to live
elsewhere. We are trying to attract them back  to this country so that we can grow the
country as a nation. Labour members say that th ey want to reduce our debt faster, but at
the same time they promise to take GST off fruit and vegetables, to immediately resume
contributions to the New Zealand Supera nnuation Fund, to increase the number of
Wellington-based bureaucrats—my goodness, th ey will be hated—to require smaller
dividends from State-owned enterprises, to establish a raft of new grants for handpicked
businesses, and to extend the paid parental leave scheme. New Zealanders should watch
out. The only way in which Labour can do that is to raise taxes and spend less as a
Government. Labour members are delusional if they think they can achieve that without
raising taxes, and that is surely the way they are headed.
The National Government has built its economic plan around six policy drivers,
including strengthening our tax system. National has delivered—

items.speaker: Brendon Burns
items.text: Tax cuts, tax cuts, tax cuts, tax cuts.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I say to Mr Burns that, yes, we have delivered on the tax cuts that
we promised. For 9 long years while Labour  was in power, when did New Zealanders
get a tax cut? Oh, that is right! It was just before the election. My goodness!

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: I wonder whether Jonathan Coleman wrote Melissa
Lee’s speech, as well. I suggest to her that  she might want to cut the ties with the
political maestro Jonathan Coleman because it is certainly not doing her any favours.
Basically, she outlined all the great po licies that Labour has already announced—
policies that the New Zealand public like, such  as paid parental leave—and said that
National opposes every single one of them.
I want to clear up something before I get in to my speech, and that is Labour’s record
in Government. I can tell Miss Lee that under Labour we had the lowest unemployment
in the OECD. We were asset-positive for th e first time. When the National Opposition
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15937
was telling us to squander our surpluses on tax cuts, we paid off debt. The debt
problems New Zealand has are largely with the private sector, because the Labour
Government did such a good job paying off Government debt. In fact, it did such a good
job that the IMF—which is not a left-wing, wonky kind of organisation—said that New
Zealand was one of the best -placed countries in the wo rld to weather the global
financial crisis because of the position that Michael Cullen and the last Labour
Government left us in. Let us get those facts straight before National spins itself out and
gets so dizzy that it cannot stand up any more with all its Crosby/Textor lines.
The legacy of this National Government after 2 years is broken promises. John Key
promised higher standards for Ministers and higher standards for MPs. What have we
had in 2 years? We have had Bill Englis h, Richard Worth, Phil Heatley, Rodney Hide,
David Garrett, Chris Finlayson, and Pansy Wong  all falling short of those standards,
with many of them having to step down from  ministerial positions  or resign from
Parliament. Also, Paula Bennett breached the Privacy Act when she viciously and cold-
heartedly released the details of welfare be neficiaries who dared to stand up in public
and question the cuts she was putting in pl ace, and the untruths she was telling about
those women. There was also the Pacific Economic Development Agency—an agency
closely linked to the National Party—which was going to get a whole whack of money
in the Budget that was not going out for tend er to anyone else, un til members on this
side of the House raised enough questions about the shonkiness of that arrangement that
the Government had to back down and put that proposal out to tender.
I will talk about another issue that has not b een raised much, and that is the issue of
MPs’ spouses being appointed to political positions. Under the Labour Government we
were quite clear that this would not ha ppen—that it was not appropriate for MPs’
spouses to be put into top political jobs. So far we ha ve seen a number of such
appointments by the National Government. I congratulate Hekia Parata, who is being
sworn in as a Minister today—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Right now.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: —right now, and I wish her al l the very best. Of course, her
husband has been appointed to a major politic al position as the head of the Tertiary
Education Commission.
The reason I raise this matter is that a number of people at home have raised
concerns with me about the regional panels for the Government’s Community Response
Fund. This fund has been set up for money to go to social service agencies to help them
deal with the recession. I cannot find anywhe re in the public domain the names of the
people who have been appointed to the panels that hand out this money. It is not on the
website. It is nowhere to be found. We have put in questions; we have not had answers
to those questions. I had a query from a me mber of the public who asked me whether it
was true that the husband of our local MP, Anne Tolley, had been appointed to the
regional panel of the Community Response Fund  for the Gisborne area. Is that true? I
do not know. I sincerely hope that it is not true. I think that would be horribly
inappropriate.
A number of social service agencies in Tai R āwhiti have been heavily criticising this
Government and Anne Tolley for the decision s they have been making. What happens
now if an organisation criticises our local MP, then she goes home and complains to her
husband about it, and suddenly that organisation is on a blacklist for the Community
Response Fund and any funding that comes from  it? I would like clarification from the
next National member to speak in this debate to guarantee that our local MP’s husband
has not been appointed to a board that is handing out money locally, because I think all
New Zealanders would deem that to be in appropriate. I look forward to that matter
being clarified. As I said, I do not know whether it is true, bu t I have had it from a very
15938 General Debate 8 Dec 2010
reliable source. In fact, I ha ve heard it from a number of  sources who say they got it
straight from the Ministry of Social Develo pment, from people who also thought that it
was very inappropriate.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: It should be public information.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: It should be public informa tion, and we should not have to
troll through the Ministry of Social Deve lopment website finding every reference to
regional panels where it is vaguely stat ed that there will be some community
representation. That is not good enough. We deserve to know who is on these panels.
We have had 2 years of broken promises fr om this Government. It promised that it
would not increase GST. The Prime Minister stared down the barrel of a TV camera
when he was asked whether he would increase  GST after the electi on, and he said that
he would not. He is now saying that he said  he would not do it to fund a deficit Budget.
Well, guess what! He did. We have a deficit Budget and a GST increase to help fund it.
It is another broken promise. The Governme nt promised that it would not borrow to
fund tax cuts—another broken promise. We have had broken promise after broken
promise.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: It has been fascinating to witness
the Labour Opposition’s rudderless and insipi d performance during the general debate
this afternoon. It will no t surprise many people who have followed Labour members’
confused and contradictory announcements of recent times that they were so reluctant to
engage with Government members over cu rrent policies, or to defend their own
irresponsible economic record when they were in Government, which contributed so
significantly to New Zealand’s slide into recession.
Labour’s record in Government is now roundly and rightly condemned by
economists, commentators, and the electorate at large. Yet what has Labour learnt? It
has learnt that Ed Miliband writes better speeches than Phil Goff. Labour members have
learnt from their embattled leader that Da vid Caygill has more credibility than their
current spokesman on finance, presumably because Mr Caygill played no role in the
economic recklessness that Labour inflicted upon New Zealand for 9 long years. They
do not seem to have learnt that Trevor Mallard should behave himself during question
time on days when he is expected to lead Labour’s “Charge of the Ultra-light Brigade”
in two measures on the same day’s Order Pa per. And, on the day when we welcome to
the House the new member for the marginal seat  of Mana, they have recently learnt that
even their previously strongest supporters are deserting them.
They are probably learning that their commitment to voodoo economics is about as
popular as their recent opposition to the package to save the Hobbit movies. It is as
credible as their commitment to higher ta xes, uncontrolled Government spending, and
welfare for millionaires.
Members on this side of the House and me mbers of the public have learnt a great
deal from Labour’s sorry and embarrassing performance both in this debate and during
today’s question time, which preceded it. We have learnt that less than a year out from a
general election Labour is in  freefall. We have learnt that Labour members lack
confidence in their leadershi p, their philosophical direction,  and in one another. They
are not just working on the basis that pixies  at the bottom of the garden will jump up
and finance their policies—as our new Poet Laureate, Aaron Gilmore, observed
earlier—but also they are increasingly turnin g to the pixies to write their policies.
Judging by how many people turn up to any of their public meetings nowadays, or take
seriously any of their utterances, it can be onl y a matter of time before their front bench
is replaced by five pixies, three goblins, and an orc. Actually, I think the orc has already
joined them, which may explain why there are so many headless chooks on their middle
and backbenches.
8 Dec 2010 General Debate 15939
I am looking forward to campaigning in Ha milton West next year on the importance
of National’s six-point plan to  growing the economy, especia lly when it is contrasted
with Labour’s six-point plan to, one, change their leader; two, lose the few electorates
they hold at the moment; and, three, increase  Government borrowing to levels that will
reduce New Zealand to a bana na-less republic. One has to wonder what they are going
to feed to the poor pixies and goblins, but I digress. The four th point is to tax anything
that moves, which means their Mana campai gn team will be all ri ght but everyone else
is in big trouble; the fifth is to bring b ack David Caygill, Fraser Colman, and Arnold
Nordmeyer; and the sixth is to hope that endless treks around the country on the magical
mystery tour, with Phil playing the ukulel e and Annette warbling “As Long as He
Needs Me”, will at least keep them away from any gathering where they might be
expected to say something credible and remotely compelling.
How ironic that David Parker should want to highlight a recent poll that put Labour
on 28 percent. How fascinating th at Labour is starting to hope that if it adds its support
to the support for New Zealand First, the Greens, Jim Anderton, and the Monster
Raving Loony Party, it might just cobble togeth er sufficient votes to get across the 5
percent MMP threshold next year. How insightful that Mr Parker spoke of losing the
plot. If I had dug a hole as deep and wide as the one he and his mates are still digging, I
would want to lose it too.
This is the last general debate of the y ear. In my usual humble fashion and in the
manner to which I have become accustomed, I am its final speaker. So it falls to me to
perform the last rites for the lacklustre, l eaderless, limp, and lamentable Labour Party. I
take the responsibility serious ly, knowing that as Michael Joseph Savage, Peter Fraser,
and Norman Kirk have spun in their graves in recent times at the shambolic efforts of
their modern day successors, the kindest act we  can all perform is to find Mr Parker’s
lost plot, ease the whole Labour caucus into it gently, and wait for some decent
opposition from the pixies, fairies, and goblins who will so surely have replaced them
by this time next year. Merry Christmas.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
First Reading

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I move, That the Westpac New Zealand Bill
be now read a first time.  This is a private bill promoted by Westpac New Zealand Ltd.
At the appropriate time, I intend to move th at this bill be refe rred to the Finance and
Expenditure Committee and that the committee report back by 8 April 2011. The bill
provides a mechanism to enable certain as sets and liabilities of Westpac Banking
Corporation in New Zealand, being principally assets a nd liabilities of Westpac
Banking Corporation’s New Zeala nd institutional banking busine ss, to be vested in its
New Zealand subsidiary, Westpac New Zealand Ltd.
Westpac is one of New Zealand’s oldest financial institutions and has operated in
New Zealand since 1861, having both a branch and a separately incorporated subsidiary,
Westpac New Zealand Ltd. Next year is its 150th anniversary in this country. It provides
key sponsorships in the community through the rescue helicopter, the Halberg Trust, the
Sir Peter Blake Trust, and Westpac Stadium, to name a few. Westpac is one of four
banks that have dual banking registration in New Zealand.
Westpac New Zealand Ltd was incorporated and became a registered bank in 2006 in
order to comply with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’ s local incorporation policy.
That incorporation policy provides that systemically important banks should be
incorporated in New Zealand. A bank is regard ed as systemically important if it has
15940 Westpac New Zealand Bill 8 Dec 2010
liabilities other than those to related part ies in excess of $15 billion. Branches of New
Zealand - registered banks, such as We stpac Banking Corporation’s New Zealand
branch, have a condition of registration that their external liabilities are not to exceed
that amount.
The Reserve Bank’s local incorporation pol icy assists the regul ator by providing it
with greater control over the assets of a bank in  the event of a bank failure under New
Zealand law. This control can help to pr event a bank failure from spilling over to the
wider financial system and developing into a systemic crisis. Having regard to that
policy, Westpac Banking Corporation and West pac New Zealand Ltd have agreed with
the Reserve Bank that Westpac Banking Corporation will transfer certain assets and
liabilities to Westpac New Zealand Ltd, bei ng principally assets and liabilities of
Westpac Banking Corporation’s New Zealand branch’s institutional banking business.
The transfer will mean that Westpac New Z ealand Ltd will increase in size, which is
beneficial in terms of the local incorporation policy, as it will allow the Reserve Bank to
have greater control over the assets that are transferred were there ever to be a failure
event. After the transfer, Westpac Banking Corporation’s New Zealand branch will
retain its financial markets operations. The transfer will reduce the size of the branch
and help to ensure that it continues to remain below the threshold going forward.
Legislation is the only means by which th e assets can be vested in Westpac New
Zealand Ltd efficiently and economically with out disrupting the conduct and continuity
of Westpac’s banking business. It  is essential for customers, staff, and other contractual
counterparties of Westpac that  the vesting is seamless. Le gislation is also the only
means by which appropriate amendments to other legislation can be made.
The bill is largely based on the Westpac New Zealand Act 2006. Li ke that Act, the
bill facilitates the vesting by providing the ov erall legal framework for the transfer of
the assets and liabilities from Westpac Ba nking Corporation to Westpac New Zealand
Ltd, with a subsequent vesting order cont aining the particulars of the assets and
liabilities to vest. Consideration was given to using the Westpac New Zealand Act 2006,
but that was not feasible, as it was not drafted with the intention of being used for a
second vesting. That is why a new Act is necessary.
The vesting of the assets and liabilities is  implemented by an Order in Council, by a
detailed proposal that must be approved by the Governor-General on the advice of the
Minister of Finance, given in accordance w ith a recommendation of the Reserve Bank.
The requirements of the proposal to be include d in the vesting order are set out in the
bill and are based closely on the Westpac New Zealand Act 2006. Given the level of
detail required to specify the assets and liabilities being vested and the fact that the
assets and liabilities of th e business are constantly chan ging, a vesting order is the
preferred means of managing this complexity.
Like the 2006 Act, a number of common me rger provisions have  been included in
the bill. The bill also ensures tax neutrality on vesting. As the transfer is being done in
order to comply with regulatory requirements, it is appropriate that no tax liability arise
or tax gain be triggered by the transfer. The Inland Revenue Department has been
consulted and is satisfied that the bill achieves the correct tax policy result. The Reserve
Bank and Treasury have been consulted and are also satisfied that the bill does not raise
any concerns from a financial stability perspective.
New Zealand has a strong and functional banki ng system. We have all seen that in
the way New Zealand has come through the gl obal financial crisis without the turmoil
in the banking sector that has been seen  offshore. Having a strong banking system
matters. I think that this bill, in a small but important way, m akes the banking system
stronger.
8 Dec 2010 Westpac New Zealand Bill 15941
I commend this private bill to the House. At  the appropriate time, I will move that it
be referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I would like to—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: A good choice.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is pretty much the only choice, I say to the chief whip.
Therefore it is a good one, if I may join the whip in expressing those sentiments.
I begin with a couple of commendations. The first is to commend the member who
has just resumed his seat, Craig Foss. Without being too pointed about it, many of us on
this side of the House think he is a very able member and he has been a very responsible
chairman of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, which is the senior select
committee. We give him a hard time around the table occasionally, but he carries it with
very good grace and business gets done. It is sensible th at the Westpac New Zealand
Bill goes to that committee.
It is ironic, then, that the member read the speech as Craig Foss and not as the Hon
Craig Foss, which many of us think he deserves  to be, and that this is a private bill, not
a Government bill. We could expect to have  heard him give a speec h like that as a new
Minister. I think it reflects ju st how concerned the Government must be about the face
of this Government, to have made the decisions it has on other matters—but that is for
another day.
There is another commendation, and that  is a commendation to Westpac New
Zealand and its colleagues in the major banks that support the New Zealand banking
industry. Whatever other comments we might  make today, we recognise the importance
to New Zealand of a strong and stable banki ng and finance sector. We certainly believe
that Westpac plays a responsible part in our financial system.
At this stage the Labour Party’s position in respect of this bill is to support the bill
being referred to select committee, and we  have an open mind be yond that. We think
that the fundamental purpose of the bill, which is to vest the institutional banking
business of Westpac Banking Corporation in to Westpac New Zealand, is appropriate.
Westpac New Zealand, of course, is a local br anch that has been set up pursuant to the
trans-Tasman regulatory structure, where by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand plays a
role as guarantor of the stability and fina ncial integrity of the New Zealand banking
system, and thereby ensures that systemi cally important banks are anchored well
enough and solidly enough in the New Zeal and market to avoid two unintended
situations. One would be a marginal market problem, in the event of a worse cataclysm
than the financial system has suffered in the last few years, if that could be imagined.
We would hate to see a situation where no t enough assets were anchored in the New
Zealand market to underpin its stability. So this is a move in that direction, and we
commend it.
With that, it is worth repeating that the idea of having a full service New Zealand -
domiciled banking regulator in the Reserv e Bank has bipartisan support around this
Chamber and is a very important part of our financial infrastructure.
Before I move through the provisions of the bi ll, I say that it is al so a little ironic to
see that the bill is in Mr Foss’ name, rather than in Nikki Kaye’s name. The convention,
of course, is that these bills are brought forward in the name of the local MP. According
to Westpac’s website, its head office and a ddress for service are in Auckland Central,
not Hawke’s Bay. One asks why the bill—

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: We have big visions for the bay.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: National does have big visions for the bay. I have a very
fond spot for the bay, as I know the bay does for me; I am well acquainted with its big
visions. None the less, why is Nikki Kaye not taking this bill to the House? Could it be
that her colleagues somehow do not  trus t her to take a bill of this substance forward to
15942 Westpac New Zealand Bill 8 Dec 2010
the House? What is it about Nikki Kaye that has meant the Government has broken with
convention and not given a private bill to the member in whose electorate the head
office of the entity concerned is domiciled? That is a break in c onvention. It is a sign,
unfortunately, that Nikki Kaye is destined to be a one-term MP, or a one-term electorate
MP anyway; of course, we look forward to  Jacinda Ardern being the new MP for
Auckland Central very shortly. I am sure th e whips would agree th at we would trust
Jacinda Ardern to bring a bill such as this  to the House—no problem at all. She has the
smarts to do it—no question.
I come back to the legislation. It is clear ly important to ensure that Westpac New
Zealand Ltd has a sound and stable New Zeal and operation while being able to enjoy
the benefits of a trans-Tasman footprin t and of access to global capital through its
Australian-based parent. We note that the success of the Reserve Bank’s local
incorporation policy is one element in securing the stability of the New Zealand banking
sector, and it is critical, as I said earlier,  that we retain sovere ign oversight of banking
regulation. The severity and speed of the 2008 financial cr isis provides ample evidence
of why it is important to do this. We can accept that the transfer of assets and liabilities
is best suited, given the complexity of the matter, to a vehicle such as this legislation.
It is also true that on both sides of the Tasman the banking sector is again under close
scrutiny. On the other side of the Ditch th e Australian Parliament has a far-reaching
inquiry under way, which brings to mind that  some of the partie s of the New Zealand
Parliament—that is, Labour, the Greens, and the Progressive part y—held an inquiry
into banking issues last year. It was a ma tter of regret that the Government’s bank,
Westpac New Zealand, did not make a submission to that inquiry. It is true that some
other banks made both formal and informal s ubmissions, and it is also true that when
the inquiry published its finding—which was that the major banks were not passing
through in full the downward changes to the o fficial cash rate into  retail and wholesale
interest rates—strangely e nough, those margins corrected th emselves within weeks of
the report being released. Imagine the coin cidence. Those margins corrected within
weeks of the report being released, saving New Zealanders tens of millions of dollars of
interest.
Of course, Labour, the Greens, and the Prog ressive party were happy to play that
service. We think it is a matter of regret, however, that the Government members of the
Finance and Expenditure Committee, after ha ving said that they would consider it,
repeatedly blocked having a banking inquiry  under the auspices of the Finance and
Expenditure Committee. There is, therefore, just a tinge of irony in the member who has
brought this bill to the House—Mr Foss, who chairs the Finance and Expenditure
Committee—now playing that role, as well as the other reasons I have suggested.
The inquiry in Australia is much broader based than being a simple matter of interest
rate pass-through. It is talking around a whole range of issues that are, to a lesser or
greater extent, also important here. The New Zealand Banking Ombudsman has said
that there were a record number of complain ts to her office over the last 12 months.
There is growing public concern about the ba nking sector. None other than Westpac’s
own chief executive now holds the record for being the highest paid chief executive in
New Zealand, eclipsing even the chief executive officer of Telecom. I used to work with
George Frazis. He is a good bloke. He is a very able executive, a nd there is no implied
negative comment about his abilities. But it is  also a matter of fact that the public
regards any individual who earns many multiples of the average salary, as the chief
executive officer of a bank like Westpac does, as a matter of some public concern.
I guess our call to the banking industry woul d be that given the climate out there,
given the fact that the New Zealand public is doing it tough, given the fact that m any
industries are struggling in the real economy, and give n that our manufacturing
8 Dec 2010 Westpac New Zealand Bill 15943
exporters have their backs against the wall with the high exchange rate, restraint is
called for. There are no plans to do an Austra lian-style banking inquiry in New Zealand
at this time, but politicians cannot ignore the growing calls from th e public to surface
issues if they continue to grow. There is a message here to the whole banking sector. It
should, please, exhibit its traditional high ethical standards and responsibilities, and play
its rightful role as pillars of the New Zealand business sector, pi llars of the economy,
and pillars of society—here not  only for today but for months and years to come—and
there will not be a problem.
I say as my final comment—I have said it publicly—that Westpac, as the
Government’s banker, has enjoyed a privileged position. The onus on it for
responsibility is higher, therefore, than on other institutions. I think we are coming close
to the time when it would be appropriate fo r the Government’s c ontract to be put up
through a transparent tender process.

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: I am very happy to rise this afternoon and take
a call on the Westpac New Zealand Bill, which is a private bill introduced by my friend
and colleague Craig Foss, who, of course , chairs the Finance and Expenditure
Committee, and does so very well.
The events of the last 2 years have really  brought into sharp focus the need for a
robust and well-respected banking  sector. Certainly in New Zealand one of the reasons
we have come through—I certainly will not say “unscathed”—in a better position than a
lot of countries is that as  we have gone through thes e difficult times our banking
system, and our banks in particular, have wo rked very well and have proven themselves
to be institutions that New Zealanders can have faith in. Nothing is more important to a
good system of financial markets in this country than for that to be the case.
A big part of that system, of  course, is the Reserve Bank an d the role it plays as both
the central bank and the prudential supervis or of the banks. I know that the Reserve
Bank took the position some time back that it is in the best interests of New Zealand and
New Zealand customers that banks that operate  in New Zealand to such an extent that
they play an important systemic role in our banking sector should largely operate as
New Zealand - registered subsidiaries, rather  than as branches of offshore banks. That
has certainly been the direc tion in which the Reserve Ba nk has encouraged banks to
move. It is not unusual by any means for ba nks to have here both subsidiaries and
branches of offshore entities. That is curre ntly how Westpac operates, and I understand
it is one of four banks that do so.
Westpac is one of our big banks in New Z ealand, and we need it to operate well and
to be in a position where, should there be an issue in the future, the Reserve Bank has
complete wraparound of the issues it needs to control as part of its regulatory oversight.
For that reason we have had the Reserve Bank institute the liabilities cap, which sets an
amount beyond which the banks cannot rise wh ile operating as branches of offshore
entities. Although Westpac has certainly always traded wi thin those requirements—and
there is no question that it does not—this bill,  with the movement of the institutional
banking sectors into Westpac New Zealand an d away from the branch operations, is
really about ensuring that no matter what volat ility is in the markets in years to come,
Westpac will be in no danger of stepping outside that cap. I know that Westpac has been
talking with the Reserve Bank on that issue for many years, and it is working with the
Reserve Bank to that end.
This bill is reasonably small in terms of its impact, but it is symptomatic of a much
wider issue that we work on in the banking sector with the Rese rve Bank, which is to
ensure, as I said, that not only do we continue to have  a strong and robust banking
sector, but also our Reserve Bank, which does such a good job of prudential oversight,
15944 Westpac New Zealand Bill 8 Dec 2010
has the ability and tools it ne eds to control all aspects of the ba nking operation, should
that be required.
Looking through the bill I see that a coupl e of things are worth commenting on so
that there is no confusion about  the extent of the powers of the bill. There are specific
provisions to ensure that customers’ relati ons are, effectively, seamlessly moved from
one part of the institution to another. The big customers currently dealing with Westpac
as a branch of the Australian company will move seamlessly through to being customers
of Westpac New Zealand without any impact at all on th em, and similarly with the
transfer of staff and the like. That is the reason a private bill is needed to achieve those
changes and to ensure that we have that  seamless transition. Ot her than a back-end
reorganisation, it will be business as usual for everyone who is dealing with Westpac.
For anyone who is listening at home and perhaps is not quite aware of the ambit of
the bill, it is worth reiterating that th e retail banking busine ss—which includes the
mums and dads and the people who use the branches and the eftpos cards—has for
many years been encapsulated within Westp ac New Zealand as a stand-alone company.
Certainly there is no reason why that would change; it will not change. Only big-
business customers dealing with the bank will be affected, and even those customers
will have their relationships entirely protected.
The other thing worth noting in closing is that the actual transfer of assets—the
specifics of what goes across—will be dete rmined by Order in Council, as has always
been the case with such matters.
It is a small and necessary bill. It is a step towards the entirely New Zealand -
incorporated banking system that the Reserve Bank is very keen on, and I am pleased to
support it.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I stand to support this pr ivate bill, the Westpac New
Zealand Bill. There are a number of reasons why we support it. It is common-sense and
absolutely necessary legislation, and Labour ha s always supported any sort of financial
legislation that we believe improves busine ss and Government efficiency. This bill is
also important to the strength of the local ba nking sector. It has already been alluded to
that Australasia came out of the financial cr isis reasonably well, and one of the reasons
we did was that we had a very strong and sound banking sector.
The bill is called the Westpac New Zealand Bill; I will just allay some people’s fears,
because we had the “Warner Bros Bill”—t he Employment Relations (Film Production
Work) Amendment Bill—earlier this year. People may think that a bill promoted by
Westpac is one of those insidious bills that is held over New Zealand by a large
international corporation. In fact, it is not at all. Whereas the “Warner Bros Bill” did
that, eroding sovereign rights of New Zealand, this bill is quite the opposite.
We support the bill, and the Reserve Bank supports it. We also understand that it is
very important that Westpac New Zealand has very sound and stable New Zealand
operations and enjoys the benefits of bei ng linked to its trans-Tasman parent—for
example, access to capital.
As mentioned, the Reserve Bank backs this bi ll. As I said, it is  a common-sense bill,
and we are very much looking forward to br inging it to the Finance and Expenditure
Committee so that we can look at its provisions and hear submissions on it, just to make
sure that it is nice and robust. But we are supporting it.
I will make one point that I think Westpac should be aware of, and that is that the
level of transparency that New Zealanders  demand of their banks is very important.
Before I elaborate on that a little further, I say that last week Westpac sent its KiwiSaver
team up to Wairoa to help out some di stressed freezing workers who had gone without
work for up to 6 months. The team did an absolutely fantastic job of providing
budgeting advice, helping people apply for some of the extreme hardship provisions that
8 Dec 2010 Westpac New Zealand Bill 15945
are available under the KiwiSaver Act, and providing a whole lot of general information
to those people in Wairoa. At this point I thank Westpac for the work it did, because it
was absolutely brilliant and it was hugely appreciated by the people of Wairoa.
We all understand the importance of a s ound banking system—of that there is no
doubt in any quarter of this H ouse. As I mentioned, our syst em held up very well, but
the one thing that is most important—and I think most New Zealanders expect if not
demand it—is a level of transparency and acco untability. Labour tried to bring that to
bear when we held our banki ng inquiry, because the vast ma jority of New Zealanders
did not understand what was happening. Probabl y there was a very logical reason for
what was happening. This was when the financia l crisis was at its height. The official
cash rate was quite low but the margins th at the banks were making were quite high,
and the vast majority of people did not understand what was going on. Labour called for
a banking inquiry. It was not supported, except by the Gr eens, and that was hugely
appreciated—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: And the Progressive party.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: —and the Progressive party, sorry. We asked the banks to appear
before us, just so they could explain in plain English what was going on, how the banks
were operating, and why they were doing what they were doing. The vast majority of
New Zealanders were suffering but banks were declaring hundreds of millions of dollars
in profit.
That was a very good opportunity to sit down in front of ordinary New Zealanders in
an open forum and get the information out th ere. Only one bank, Kiwibank, sat down in
front of us and explained. Westpac did not, and I say to We stpac, as the Government
banker, that we demand a level of accountabil ity and responsibility, especially from the
Government’s banker, and we hope that in  future Westpac takes advantage of any
opportunity to explain to the public its methods of operation.
We are supporting this bill, and I look forw ard to its going to the select committee.
But also I say to Westpac that there is an element of disquiet in the country at the
moment about the situation where the New Zealand chief executive of Westpac—who is
earning about $5 million, I think—has just re ceived a tax cut of about $5,000 per week,
and the person who cleans his office has received a tax cut of about $5 a week, which is
about 1,000 times smaller than the tax cut the chief executive is getting. A lot of New
Zealanders have a level of disquiet about that situation. But th is is a good bill. We
support it, and I look forward to it coming before the select committee. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I stand on behalf of the Greens to
speak on the Westpac New Zealand Bill, which is a private bill coming before this
House, taking House time, and using quite a lot of public money. The Greens will
support this bill to go to select committee but  we will not necessarily support it further
until we look at it at the select committee.
Westpac is, of course, one of the oli gopoly players in the New Zealand banking
system. One of the things that became very  clear during the Multi-party Parliamentary
Banking Inquiry was that we do not have a very competitive banking market in New
Zealand, aside from Kiwibank, because the four pillars of the Australian banking
system are present in New Zealand. They had a cosy arrangement, at least before
Kiwibank turned up, where they did not comp ete on price. The market was divided up
and they sought to maximise their profits, which they sent back to Australia, rather than
competing on price.
That arrangement was indicated in some of the evidence that was presented to us by
Kiwibank at the inquiry. Those who do not really understand the banking sector—
which, I suspect, includes a lot of the National m embers—do not realise that the
banking sector worked through a cosy arrang ement involving the big Australian banks,
15946 Westpac New Zealand Bill 8 Dec 2010
and there was no serious competition on price. That is one of the problems we have in
dealing with it. Having basically let the banki ng sector slip into overseas ownership, we
have this ongoing problem.
We also have an issue with Westpac and th e big Australian banks in respect of their
tax avoidance activities. On 23 December last year the big Australian banks were forced
to pay back nearly $2 billion to the New Z ealand taxpayer—$2 billion in taxes that they
had unlawfully avoided. They were caught out by the Inland Revenue Department and
lost their cases in the New Zealand High Court. The banks fought their cases as far as
they could, and then, on 23 December—which , for those who do not know, is 2 days
before Christmas, when most people are rather busy doing other things—the
announcement was made that the banks had agr eed to pay back the money, or at least
some of it. They did not pay back all the money they owed, and they did not have any
penalties, unlike ordinary taxpayers. No one from Westpac or from the other banks was
charged with anything. None the less, they  agreed to pay back a good chunk of the
money that they had unlawfully avoided.
We are pretty cynical about the behaviour  of Westpac and th e other banks, having
seen their behaviour in actively and unlawfully avoiding very, very large amounts of tax
that they owed the New Zealand taxpayer. We have a slightly cynical approach towards
Westpac.
Of course, because we have these foreign- owned banks we also have the problem of
huge amounts of profit being transferred back overseas. The biggest part of New
Zealand’s current account deficit is in the investment income deficit, and that is because
of the profits that are going back to the overseas owners—large ly Australian-based
overseas owners—which adds significantl y to the current account deficit in New
Zealand.
In fact, in the middle of th e global financial crisis the Australian banks were
transferring more money out of New Zealand than they were actually making in profits.
It is one of the untold stories of the crisis that while we were effectively subsidising the
banks by providing a wholesale and retail gua rantee for them, they were shovelling
money back across to their owners as fast as  they could, to make sure that the balance
sheets back in Australia looked good. Wh ile the New Zealand taxpayers were
subsidising the Australian banks, basically because we gave them cheap insurance—and
they would have been in trouble had the taxpa yers not provided a wholesale and retail
guarantee—the banks were shovelling money back to their owners. That provided a real
problem for New Zealand. During the global financial crisis, capital was extremely
short, so having the banks send the money back to Australia was a big problem.
We also have an issue with Westpac a nd the other banks around the treatment of
staff. Basically, Westpac and other banks incen tivise their staff to put people into debt.
They have staff incentives where staff get paid bonuses if they can convince people to
add more money on to their credit cards, or to increase their credit card limits, which
just creates further debt problems for New Zealanders.
The other issue specific to Westpac is around the master banking agreement. The last
time the agreement was put out for open tender was when David Lange was Prime
Minister; we have not had an open tender fo r that agreement since then. There have
been some negotiations with Westpac, but it is very difficult for us to be sure that we
are getting a very good deal  out of Westpac when th ere has been no open tender
agreement.
Finally, of course, there is the issue of pa y. The chief executive officer of Westpac is
given $5 million a year out of the pockets of  Westpac customers. They ultimately have
to pay that $5 million a year. I think it is grossly inequitable that someone in New
Zealand is paid $5 million a year. I think that Westpac should look at itself.
8 Dec 2010 Westpac New Zealand Bill 15947

items.speaker: BRENDON BURNS
items.text: Labour supports the
Westpac New Zealand Bill going to the Finance and Expenditure Committee. We want
to see a very strong banking sector. It is f undamental to our economy. It is also a fact of
life that our banking sector is dominated by the four major Australian-owned banks.
They hold more than 90 percent of the banking transaction market. It is to the credit of
those Australian-owned banks that over the la st few years we have seen what I suppose
is more restrained lending in our nation than  in other parts of th e world. Members can
refer to Ireland currently, where the banking s ector is at the heart of the financial
collapse leading to savage public funding cuts and a rescue package led by the European
Union.
But the Australian-owned banks are not all c overed in glory. Of course, in a number
of sectors here there has b een lending beyond what is appropriate, an d there have been
some fairly strong views voiced that the Australian-owned banks, including Westpac,
were riding interest rates—and perhaps are still riding interest rates—in the wake of the
losses they have sustained in the face of the global financial meltdown. That is why it
was important that the Australian-owned  banks, including Westpac, should have
supported the Labour-Greens inquiry into the banking sector , an inquiry that was set up
only because the Government refused to have a wider, officially sanctioned review of
the banking sector. As we know, Westpac did not support that review, nor did any of its
colleague Australian-owned banks. We do not hold that against Westpac, but it might
give further thought to supporting any future reviews.
I would also like to comment on the issue of  the chief executive’s salary. Frankly, it
is unacceptable for the pay package of a ch ief executive of any institution—be it public
or privately owned—when we ar e still in the toughest economic times in a generation,
to be worth more than 100 times the value, th e cost, the income of some of the staff he
is representing. There is an extraordinary disparity between  what the ordinary workers
are receiving and what the chief executive—who, even when all due credit is paid, is on
a very, very high salary package—is earn ing. When we consider that the average
Westpac customer support worker is earning from around $45,000—that is, 124 th of the
package that the Westpac chief executive is  receiving—we see that there is a huge
disparity.
It brings to mind that questions are star ting to be asked around the world about pay
equity. In Britain the Tory Government, the new David Cameron - led Government, has
established a review of pay equity led by none other than a fellow called Will Hutton,
who is a staunch Labour supporter and well- known commentator and journalist. That
review is going through some of the issues that have seen these kinds of extortionate
salary levels paid to senior figures, and the disparity between those salaries and those of
ordinary people earning ordinary incomes. The review is getting very wide support from
some surprising figures, one of them bei ng Michael Portillo, a former Thatcherite
Cabinet Minister, who has ac knowledged that when market reforms were set in place
under the Thatcher administration there was an expectation that the private sector would
show some restraint, that the gap between those on the top, thos e at the bottom, and
those in the middle would not grow and grow and grow. Unfo rtunately, that is what we
saw in Britain, and that is what we see in New Zealand today.
Labour members support this bill going to the Finance and Expenditure Committee
for further review; that is appropriate. We support this legislati on, but we do so in a
spirit that says the Westpac chief executive ne eds to consider the equity of his salary
package. There are issues involved there as far as many New Zealanders are concerned.
Ultimately, the customer is right. Ultimately, th ose sorts of issues can have an impact
upon the choices that consumers make in the market. I woul d note that other bank chief
15948 Westpac New Zealand Bill 8 Dec 2010
executives’ salary packages are around half the level, or th ereabouts, of that enjoyed by
the Westpac chief executive.
I would like to comment very briefly on one other issue in respect of Westpac. One
of its major call centres is sited in my el ectorate of Christchurch Central. There are
some question marks still about the future of that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I will take just a short call on the
Westpac New Zealand Bill. I congratulate Cr aig Foss on bringing it forward for its first
reading, and we look forward to its going to the Finance and Expenditure Committee. I
am sure that his leadership of the select co mmittee will be invaluable as the bill is taken
through it.
We look forward to all parties supporting the bill as it goes through the committee
process. [ Interruption] Why? Well, I think it is importa nt that we recognise that the
banking sector has been crucial to New Z ealand as it traverses this very difficult
economic time. It may be opportune for some  of the political part ies on the Opposition
side to whack the banking sector around a bit for the sake of scoring easy political
points, but, effectively, one  of the few differences be tween New Zealand and those
Western countries that have found these times difficult has been our strong banking
sector. That banking sector is dominated by the four big Australian banks, and those
banks have been invaluable in providi ng New Zealand with economic safety during
these very troubled times.
I think that if we can engage in something that will assist that banking sector, then
that is important and is in the best intere sts of New Zealanders and of the economy as a
whole. That is why it is important that al l parties support this bill. The focus is not
purely on just one of the banks; this bill is about Westpac, of course, but we want to
make sure we also look after the other three big banks, which have also provided a lot of
security to this country over th e last couple of year s. It is unfortunate that members of
the Opposition have used this  bill to talk about management policies within Westpac,
rather than actually looking at the bill, which has nothing to do with the chief
executive’s employment.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: You would never do that, would you, David?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: No, we would never do that, because we would stick to the
nature of the bill, unlike parties over ther e, which are there just for political point-
scoring, and not for genuinely attempting to make this country better. That is something
that that new member will learn—that Labour is not here to give genuine help to New
Zealanders. He has been here about 5 minut es and thinks he can tell us what Labour
actually would do. We have seen Labour me mbers operate in good and bad times, and
they do not care about New Zealand. They neve r have and never will.  It is all about
themselves, and this debate is just anothe r example. They have gone after the chief
executive rather than supporting a bill that  would promote a company that has been
invaluable in helping us getting through the recession.
It is very important that all parties support the bill, and I think that as it goes through
the select committee process we will see that they do support it. It is interesting that the
Green Party is represented on the select comm ittee, and I am sure that Russel will take
an active interest in this bill and be construc tive in the way that the issue is dealt with.
Labour members on the committee may focus on the wording of reports rather than the
actual nature of the bill, but that is the nature of how they operate.
In essence, this bill is important for the W estpac bank to retain its ability to operate
and function in a way that supports the Ne w Zealand economy. We look forward to it
going through this House in a very successful manner. It will be in the best interests of
8 Dec 2010 Westpac New Zealand Bill 15949
New Zealand, and that is something Labour members are yet to work out. They will
take some time to do so, because they are not thinking along those lines. Thank you.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: It is somewhat ironic to be able to stand and do a
bill about Westpac—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: It’s your bill?

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: —talk about a bill on Westpac—sorry, Mr Hughes. This bill
has been brought to the House by Craig Foss, the wonderful member from Tukituki.
Westpac was my first bank, and I vividly re member, as a 7-year-old, going to New
Brighton and opening up my first bank account with Westpac. It was not called Westpac
at that stage; it was actually called Trust Bank Canterbury. I raise that because it relates
to a really interesting aspect of the reason for this bill havi ng to be brought before the
House. Westpac bought out Trust Bank Canterbu ry, as some other members may recall.
Trust Bank Canterbury was the dominant bank in Christchurch and in the wider South
Island. All of the assets that were purchased as part of the acquisition of Trust Bank
Canterbury ended up going into what was called the Westpac Banking Corporation
branch, which actually was a branch of the Australian operation, not a stand-alone
entity. At the time people thought “Well, so what?”. The big, key aspect of that was that
the depositors and investors in  Trust Bank Canterbury went from being investors in a
direct subsidiary of a New Zealand entity—that is, it was regulated by the Reserve Bank
of New Zealand—to being investors in a branch entity, over which the Reserve Bank
had less control. The bill we have before us actually fixes that, and I think that is a good
step.
Westpac has been in New Zealand for a long time. As I say, the personal history of
my banking relationship with them has been an  interesting one. But the bank has been a
good customer and operator in New Zealand. Westpac has been very good in terms of
the recent earthquake in Canterbury, and has worked very well with  the locals there.
That is a good indication of  how well Westpac operates w ithin our wider financial
community. But this bill actually makes so me improvements. As we have seen, there
are some issues, potentially, with it operating as a branch of an Australian bank, rather
